episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of J. H. Floyd took place in Arizona Territory in May 1881, when armed men from Florence pursued Sheriff J. P. Gabriel and his prisoner to Casa Grande and demanded Floyd at gunpoint. Floyd had been arrested for shooting dead an elderly Florence resident, Charles Bernard, known as "American Charley." The sheriff held off the party until a train arrived and lodged Floyd in the Tucson jail; Floyd was later convicted of manslaughter, a verdict Arizona papers denounced so sharply that one regretted the lynching had failed.

episodes.title: Killing of Jerry Hamilton
episodes.lead: The killing of Jerry Hamilton was the fatal beating of a Black plantation worker by masked men near Red Bluff, Montgomery County, Georgia, on the night of May 2, 1881. A mass meeting at Mount Vernon denounced it, and in June ten local men were brought to Savannah on a federal civil rights warrant.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Jim Myers from Newark Valley
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Jim Myers from Newark Valley was the forced departure, in late May or early June 1881, of Jim Myers (also spelled Meyers) and, by one account, a French partner from their cabin at Antelope Springs, Nevada, after stockmen ordered them out under threat of lynching. The men left without violence, and Nevada papers treated the episode as a brief item of local news.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Patton (Potter)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Patton (also reported as John Potter) was the killing of a prisoner charged with horse stealing, who was taken from a deputy sheriff on the road near Kerrville, Texas, in May 1881 and shot dead. No one was identified, and the case reached papers outside Texas as an example of Texas "lawlessness".

episodes.title: Lynching of Matt Butts
episodes.lead: The lynching of Matt Butts was the hanging of a Black man by a mob near Arlington, Early County, Georgia, on or about May 31, 1881. Butts had been accused of stabbing Maj. W. J. Bethea to death, and after his capture he was taken by a mob, reported as 200 men, and hanged to a tree. An Atlanta wire carried the news to papers in the Midwest and West, while a Georgia paper passed on a local account that called him Matt Horton.

episodes.title: Killing of the McKinney family on Kinney Creek
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The killing of the McKinney family on Kinney Creek was an attack in late May 1881 in which regulators broke into a family's house on Kinney Creek in Carter County, Kentucky, and killed a man and two women named McKinney. It was reported as one of a series of regulator crimes in northeastern Kentucky, and one paper said the family was killed because they refused to be driven from the country. No report gives the victims' first names or race.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Jesse Myers and Frank Brown
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Jesse Myers and Frank Brown took place at New Madrid, Missouri, in late May 1881, when a mob organized to hang the two men, accused members of an outlaw gang, after they were brought to the town jail. Before the mob could act, Sheriff Walters and a few assistants removed the prisoners after dark and took them by river to St. Louis. The threat arose during a widely reported manhunt in southeast Missouri; Myers and Brown were later tried and hanged legally at New Madrid on July 15, 1881.

episodes.title: Lynching of Pat Rhodes
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Pat Rhodes was the hanging of a wounded prisoner near Bayne's store, between New Madrid and Sikeston, Missouri, on the morning of May 12, 1881. Rhodes was one of four men accused of shooting into William Knox's house and killing a member of the posse sent after them. The wire said vigilantes hanged him, while local letters said only that he was found hanging in a stable while under guard.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of Pete Megley
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of Pete Megley was a hanging that Nevada papers said had taken place in the cattle valleys of White Pine County in about May 1881, when Megley and another man were rumored to have been found hanging from a tree. Reports blamed ranchmen who suspected the men of cattle stealing, but the story was retracted, revived and denied over several weeks, and no body, inquest or arrest was reported. No report gives the race of either man.

episodes.title: Lynching of Billy Leroy and Sam Potter
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Billy Leroy and Sam Potter took place at Del Norte, Colorado, apparently on the night of May 22, 1881, when a party of men took the two captured stage robbers from the town jail and hanged them. Leroy, an escaped mail robber, and Potter had been brought to Del Norte as prisoners, and briefs printed across the country said they were lynched by citizens within an hour of arrival. A later account said a coroner's jury exonerated all concerned and that the dead men were brothers named Pond.

episodes.title: Lynching at the Talladega picnic (1881)
episodes.lead: The lynching at the Talladega picnic was the hanging of an unnamed Black man near Talladega, Alabama, in May 1881, by the father and fellow members of a picnic party who accused him of choking the father's young daughter to death and robbing her. He was hanged to a tree near the falls of a river and his body was left hanging. The story ran across the country as a wire item, often under headlines that approved of the killing, such as 'Justifiable Lynching'.

episodes.title: Reported torture of Abner Stanley and James Tibbetts
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The reported torture of Abner Stanley and James Tibbetts was a June 1881 episode in which, according to wire dispatches, fifteen to twenty armed men took four men from their homes in or near Sharp County, Arkansas, one Thursday night and tortured them in a glen to make them confess a robbery. Dispatches from Little Rock said Tibbetts and Stanley could not be found and were feared to have been tortured to death, while the other two men were jailed on suspicion of the robbery. Three weeks later the Sharp County Record denied that anything of the kind had happened in its part of the state.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Albert Hayes
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Albert Hayes took place at about one o'clock in the morning of June 7, 1881, when a body of masked men broke into the county jail at Cairo, Illinois, to take and hang Hayes, a young Black prisoner. The men broke through a door and two of three cell locks but dispersed after the jail's keeper confronted them and fire bells were rung, and Hayes was held for trial.

episodes.title: Shooting of Allen and Alex Philips
episodes.lead: The shooting of Allen and Alex Philips took place on Sunday afternoon, 12 June 1881, when a deputy sheriff's party trying to arrest Allen Philips, a Black man, shot both brothers at Alex's house on Dr. Huguet's plantation below Baton Rouge, Louisiana. Both men were wounded, and a physician judged the wounds not fatal. The Baton Rouge Louisiana Capitolian reported the officers' version in full and declared them "fully justified," and the story reached other Louisiana papers as a one-line exchange item.

episodes.title: Killing of Allen Chapman
episodes.lead: The killing of Allen Chapman was the shooting of a Black man by a band of masked, armed men at his cabin in Haywood district, Chattooga County, Georgia, on the night of about June 6, 1881. The band had come for a white girl who lived with him, and when Chapman met them with a shotgun they opened fire; he was reported dead. A Columbus dispatch carried in the Wheeling Intelligencer under the headline "Murder by Georgia Regulators" is the only known report.

episodes.title: Threats against Anderson Johnson (Bath County, Kentucky, 1881)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threats against Anderson Johnson followed his killing of his cousin Isaac Alfrey in Bath County, Kentucky, in early June 1881, and drove Johnson from his home under a warning of death. A widely reprinted wire brief said a mob had gone to hang him, but the Kentucky reports describe a court examination and an anonymous notice to leave rather than a mob. No report gives the race of either man.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Bart Philips
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Bart Philips took place in Woodstock, Shenandoah County, Virginia, on the night of June 6, 1881, when a party of citizens formed to hang Philips, a Black man suspected of setting fire to the stables behind Welsh's Hotel. Philips was kept out of the crowd's reach, quietly arrested and committed to jail to await indictment.

episodes.title: Lynching of Cal Emory
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Cal Emory took place about midnight on the night of June 13, 1881, when about twenty-five armed men forced the county jail at Dover, Pope County, Arkansas, shot Emory in his cell and hanged him on a gallows. Emory had been convicted of murdering a woman in Franklin County and sentenced to death, but Governor Churchill had commuted the sentence to twenty-one years in the penitentiary a few weeks earlier. It was the third attempt to lynch him, and Arkansas papers largely excused it as a rebuke to the governor's pardons.

episodes.title: Killing of Dennis Brothen
episodes.lead: The killing of Dennis Brothen took place on the night of June 1, 1881, when a party of four young white men came to the home of Brothen, a Black man, in Camp County, Texas, near Jefferson, and two of them killed him. Brothen had fired on the party, killing Calvin Cope and mortally wounding Israel Hagrand, and the two unhurt men escaped. A brief dispatch from Jefferson carried the story to papers from West Virginia to California and Montana within a week.

episodes.title: Manhunt for Charles Gilmor
episodes.lead: The manhunt for Charles Gilmor took place around Martinsville in June 1881, when posses of citizens hunted Gilmor, a Black man, after he was accused of trying to rape Miss Winchester in her father's house. No capture or violence against him was reported, but the Chicago Daily Tribune printed the news under a headline saying such men should be hanged when caught.

episodes.title: Burning of the Black schoolhouse at Empire, Kentucky
episodes.lead: The burning of the Black schoolhouse at Empire, Kentucky, was an arson in early June 1881 in which 'some unknown parties' set fire to a 'negro school house' at the coal-mining settlement of Empire. No one was reported hurt and no arrests were reported, but the Hopkinsville South Kentuckian called those responsible 'scoundrels' who were 'unfit to live' and urged that they be prosecuted.

episodes.title: Lynching of Estes Hairston and Lindsay
episodes.lead: The lynching of Estes Hairston and Lindsay was the hanging of two Black prisoners by about 150 masked men who took them from the jail at Danbury, Stokes County, North Carolina, on the night of Monday, June 20, 1881. Both had been held for months awaiting trial on charges of raping a white girl and a white woman. Wire reports said the hanging was generally approved, and a local correspondent published a defense of it.

episodes.title: Killing of Frank Matterson and two horse thieves at Rock Creek
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The killing of Frank Matterson and two horse thieves at Rock Creek was the reported shooting of Matterson, called "Big Frank", and the hanging of two unnamed men, all three accused of stealing horses in North Park, in about June 1881. The only known account, a brief item in the Cheyenne Daily Leader, rested on hearsay and said the people of the park felt "justly revenged."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of George Hadington
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of George Hadington took place at Savannah, Tennessee, in late June 1881, after Hadington, a Black man, was arrested on a charge of attempting to assault a fourteen-year-old white girl. The only report found, a brief in the Memphis Daily Appeal, said that the arrest caused "considerable excitement" and that threats to lynch him had been made, but it reported no attack.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Taylor at Greensboro
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Taylor at Greensboro took place on the night of Monday, June 6, 1881, when, according to the Raleigh Observer, a large party of armed men rode into Greensboro, North Carolina, to take Taylor, a Black prisoner, from the Guilford County jail. Taylor was accused of raping a white woman, Mrs. James Irwin, near Reidsville in Rockingham County, and the sheriff removed him from the jail before the men could reach him. The attempt followed a raid on the Rockingham County jail at Wentworth, and five days later a larger party broke into the Greensboro jail, took Taylor out and hanged him.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Henry Purnell
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Henry Purnell took place near Tuckerman, Arkansas, on June 20, 1881, when a posse of citizens that had hunted him all day for an alleged rape captured him in the woods and nearly hanged him. Purnell, a farm hand of about sixty, was instead jailed, pleaded guilty before a justice the next morning, and was held under guard amid threats of lynching. The case reached papers from Memphis to Idaho through an Arkansas Gazette special and a shorter wire brief, none of which stated anyone's race.

episodes.title: Lynching of three Black men at Rolling Fork Creek, Sevier County, Arkansas
episodes.lead: The lynching of three Black men at Rolling Fork Creek took place in early June 1881 near Locksburg (also spelled Lockesburg), Sevier County, Arkansas, when armed white men hanged three unnamed men accused of robbing and murdering a farmer, R. F. Hall. The men were caught in a manhunt and hanged from trees at the ford where Hall had been killed, the last two on the night of Tuesday, June 7. Dispatches from Little Rock carried the story across the country under headlines such as "Speedy Justice" and "Just Retribution."

episodes.title: Killing of J. E. Martin
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The killing of J. E. Martin was the murder of a merchant at Belknap, Texas, who was called from his house by three men on the night of June 9, 1881, led about half a mile away and shot dead. The men then robbed his store, and about two weeks later three men named McDonald were jailed at Graham for the crime amid fears that Belknap citizens would lynch them.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jeff (Louisiana, 1881)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jeff was the hanging of a Black man in Louisiana in late June 1881, after he was accused of attacking the daughter of W. R. Turnage, his employer. The Farmerville Gazette's account, reprinted in three Louisiana papers, defended the killing as a case that did not admit of "law's delay."

episodes.title: Killing of Jeff Hill
episodes.lead: The killing of Jeff Hill was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Constable J. M. Senac in Justice Langlois' court at New Iberia, Louisiana, on a Monday in June 1881, most likely June 6, while Hill was being tried on his wife's complaint that he had beaten her. Senac surrendered and was released on $500 bail, and a guard was placed at the jail after a rumor that Black residents meant to lynch him.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Jesus Leon
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Jesus Leon was an effort in June 1881 at San Juan Capistrano, California, to lynch Leon, a man described as "a Mexican" who was accused of stabbing Enlogio Alvarez to death. Officers prevented the attempt and took Leon to jail in Los Angeles, where he was charged with murder the following month.

episodes.title: "An Episode of Border Life" (lynching of a gambler called Jim)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: "An Episode of Border Life" is a first-person sketch, credited to the Pittsburgh Post and reprinted in the Somerset Press of Ohio on 16 June 1881, describing the lynching of a gambler called Jim by miners in an unnamed Western mining town. In the story, fifteen or twenty men left a coroner's inquest, broke into the jail and hanged the gambler for shooting a police officer, then posed for a photograph with the body. The sketch gives no date, place, surname or race, and no other report of the episode appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of circus workers in Chesaning, Michigan
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of circus workers in Chesaning, Michigan, took place on June 8, 1881. A mob of about 300 townspeople tried to lynch four employees of a traveling circus who were held in connection with the killing of a village policeman. A posse of twelve men held the crowd back with revolvers and put the prisoners on a train to Saginaw City. Two of the four, Sim Robinson and William Murray, were described as "colored"; the case reached readers mainly through Chicago Tribune dispatches and Michigan state-news columns.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Taylor
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Taylor took place on the night of June 11-12, 1881, when masked, mounted men broke into the Guilford County jail at Greensboro, North Carolina, and carried off Taylor, a Black farm hand accused of raping a white woman near Reidsville. They hanged him from a roadside oak in Rockingham County, and a coroner's jury found he had been hanged by unknown parties. A Danville wire report noting that the raid came during an eclipse of the moon ran across the country, while North Carolina papers mostly approved the lynching.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Taylor
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Taylor took place before dawn on June 12, 1881, when a large party of men took Taylor, a young Black farm hand, from the Greensboro, North Carolina, jail and hanged him by a road about seven miles from Reidsville in Rockingham County. Taylor and George Gunn had been accused of assaulting the wife of Col. James Irwin on June 3, and an attempt to lynch them at the Wentworth jail on June 5 had failed. North Carolina papers largely endorsed the killing, and a Danville wire carried it nationally as a lynching done during an eclipse of the moon.

episodes.title: Lynching of Josh Shorter
episodes.lead: The lynching of Josh Shorter was the hanging of a Black man by a crowd near Eufaula, Alabama, on June 9, 1881. Shorter, accused of assaulting a young white girl the day before, was captured across the river in Georgia and hanged from a tree after a crowd kept him from the sheriff. The Savannah Morning News headlined the news "Speedy Vengeance," and a brief wire item carried it to papers as far away as Utah and California.

episodes.title: Lynching of Juan Monterea
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Juan Monterea was the hanging of a man accused of murder by a group of men in Taos County, New Mexico Territory, on the night of Saturday, June 11, 1881. Monterea had been arrested and jailed after Leon M. Gallagher, who had objected to his treatment of his mother, was killed with a hoe. According to a Santa Fe dispatch, a "large body of men" took him from jail and hanged him from the railing of the courthouse. The story ran as a short wire item in papers across the country in the following two weeks.

episodes.title: Lynching of Reimheimer
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Reimheimer was the hanging of a German man, his name printed as Reimheimer and in several other spellings, by a band of about twenty to twenty-five unknown men who took him from the jail at Rockport, Atchison County, Missouri, early on June 11, 1881. He had been accused of shooting and robbing a man named Albert Angel near Irish Grove six days earlier, and he was awaiting trial when he was seized. A St. Joseph dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, often in news summaries beside the lynching of a Black man, John Taylor, in North Carolina the same weekend.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jim Connors
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jim Connors took place at Espanola, New Mexico Territory, in June 1881, when masked men took Connors, accused with Harry Knowles of shooting a storekeeper in an attempted robbery, from his guards at night and hanged him from a telegraph pole. Knowles had already been shot dead by a citizens' party pursuing the pair. A wire report carried the episode across the country as the swift punishment of New Mexico "desperadoes", and no article in the coverage gives the race of either man.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Daniel McDonald
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Daniel McDonald took place at Ludington, Michigan, in early June 1881, when a crowd met him at the steamboat landing as officers brought him in on a charge of murdering a boy at a sawmill. The crowd called for him to be lynched, but no organized attempt was made and the sheriffs jailed him.

episodes.title: Perry County Ku-Klux threats and Perryville newspaper fire
episodes.lead: The Perry County Ku-Klux threats and Perryville newspaper fire were a campaign of death threats, arson and armed intimidation at Perryville, Arkansas, in May and June 1881 against County Judge L. M. Harris, editor John L. Matthews and others by a group signing itself the "regular organized Ku-Klux." On a Sunday night, June 5 by the first dispatches, the newspaper office was set on fire; citizens put out the flames. Harris and Matthews fled before armed men came asking for them, and Governor Churchill sent General R. C. Newton to investigate. Matthews was shot dead outside his office in July in what dispatches called the same troubles.

episodes.title: Lynching of Robert Frye
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Robert Frye was the hanging of a man described as a horse thief, whose body was found in the woods near Arlington, Texas, on a Tuesday evening in mid-June 1881. His killers left a placard reading "Horse thief" on the body and were not identified. The killing reached distant readers only as a one-sentence item in national news-brief columns.

episodes.title: Rose Hill attempted lynching (1881)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Rose Hill attempted lynching was an attempt by citizens in early June 1881 to lynch one of three white men accused of assaulting a blacksmith's daughter at Rose Hill, Lee County, apparently in Virginia. After capturing the man across the state line in Tennessee, his pursuers brought him back to the scene of the crime and prepared to lynch him; the only report does not say what followed.

episodes.title: Lynching of Charles Diddell
episodes.lead: The lynching of Charles Diddell was the hanging of a Black man by a mob from a bridge at Weston, Platte County, Missouri, on the evening of Sunday, June 12, 1881. Diddell, whose name was also printed "Didell," had been jailed that day, accused of raping and trying to kill a young white woman, and the mob took him from the jail and hanged him without trial. Papers from Chicago to Savannah carried the story; one wire brief named the victim "Ruse" and said his head was cut off after the hanging.

episodes.title: Tracy City cabin shooting
episodes.lead: The Tracy City cabin shooting was an attack on June 11, 1881, in which unknown parties fired into the cabin of a Black man at Tracy City, Tennessee. No deaths or injuries were reported, and the case drew notice because Governor Hawkins offered a reward for the attackers.

episodes.title: Lynching of Sidney King
episodes.lead: The lynching of Sidney King was the hanging of a Black youth by local residents in Hernando County, Florida, in late June or early July 1881. King was accused of shooting and cutting the three children of Sheriff J. Bart Mickler and robbing the sheriff's house, and he was hanged before a crowd reported as 200 citizens. A Jacksonville dispatch carried the story across the country, and papers in the South and North treated the hanging as deserved punishment.

episodes.title: Shooting of Victor Davidson
episodes.lead: The shooting of Victor Davidson was a street shooting in Charlotte, North Carolina, on the night of Monday, June 20, 1881, in which one of three young white men fired at two Black men and wounded Davidson in the forehead. Davidson's condition was not known when the story appeared, and it was reported in his home town of Yorkville, South Carolina, because he had lived there.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Utley and Henry Fisher
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Utley and Henry Fisher took place at Springfield, Tennessee, in late June 1881, after the two Black men were jailed on the night of June 27 on a charge of attempting to assault a white woman, Mrs. Mattie Davis. A Nashville dispatch predicted they would be lynched before morning, and a later brief said the people of Springfield had made preparations to lynch them. No report of the outcome was found.

episodes.title: Shooting of Will Wilkerson
episodes.lead: The shooting of Will Wilkerson took place at Malvern, Arkansas, on or about June 19, 1881, when a town marshal named Hall dangerously wounded Wilkerson, a Black man, while trying to arrest him. Wilkerson escaped to the woods and was still at large when the news was telegraphed from Little Rock the next day, with a number of people pursuing him.

episodes.title: Search for William Gauch
episodes.lead: The search for William Gauch was a manhunt by "citizens" of the county around Hillsboro, North Carolina, in late June 1881 for a Black man accused of raping a 10-year-old girl. The only report found, a Greensboro dispatch in the Chicago Daily Tribune, ended with the search under way and printed it under the headline "WRETCHES WHO SHOULD BE HUNG WHEN CAUGHT."

episodes.title: Beating of William Green by Shreveport police
episodes.lead: The beating of William Green by Shreveport police took place in Shreveport, Louisiana, in mid-June 1881, when Policeman Wimbish struck Green, a Black man wanted for larceny, several times over the head with his pistol during his arrest. A crowd of Black residents gathered and threatened to free Green, and the police chief ordered the arrest of its leaders. The only account is a Shreveport Times item, reprinted twice in a Baton Rouge paper, that tells the story from the officer's side.

episodes.title: Grand Haven jail mob of 1881
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Grand Haven jail mob of 1881 was an attempted lynching in June 1881, when a dozen or more farmers broke into the jail at Grand Haven, Ottawa County, Michigan, to hang a prisoner named Voskamp who was accused of murder. The sheriff's wife locked the mob inside the jail, and seven of its leaders later pleaded guilty to assault and were fined $100 each. Newspapers across the country told it as a comic story about lynchers who were themselves captured.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Albert Hoyt
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Albert Hoyt took place at Astoria, Oregon, on the night of July 7, 1881, when a large crowd gathered at the town jail with a rope prepared to hang Hoyt, a longshoreman accused of raping a nine-year-old girl. The police chief refused to bring the prisoner out and guarded the jail, and Hoyt was later sentenced to twenty years in the penitentiary. Pacific Coast papers carried the case as a crime story in which a lynching was narrowly avoided.

episodes.title: Big Sandy railroad regulators, Carter County, Kentucky (1881)
episodes.lead: The Big Sandy railroad regulators were a gang in Carter County, Kentucky, led by the brothers David and William Patton, who in the summer of 1881 were reported to be driving workmen off the Big Sandy railroad. On 20 July 1881 the county judge asked Governor Blackburn for help, and the governor sent a general to the scene and offered rewards for the brothers' capture. One wire report described the workmen as "colored" and said several had been killed and others whipped, but the fuller dispatch carried by most papers named no race and no deaths.

episodes.title: Assault on Bill Hackney
episodes.lead: The assault on Bill Hackney was an attack on a Black man during an affray between white and Black men at Columbia, Virginia, reported in early July 1881, in which he was struck on the head with a pick-handle and thrown from a window fifteen feet above the ground. The incident is known only from a one-sentence wire brief that ran in crime columns of Midwestern weeklies, which gave no cause, assailant or outcome.

episodes.title: Killing of an unidentified Black man at the Blanco River, Hays County
episodes.lead: The killing of an unidentified Black man at the Blanco River took place on July 29, 1881, when a deputy sheriff of Hays County, Texas, shot him dead near the railroad bridge over the river. The deputy was said to have fired because the man resisted arrest, and neither man's name reached the press. The killing is known from a single brief Austin dispatch whose headline called the dead man a cattle thief, a charge the dispatch itself did not make.

episodes.title: Burning of the Black church at Cedar Grove, Alabama
episodes.lead: The burning of the Black church at Cedar Grove, Alabama, was an arson attack on the church of a Black congregation at Cedar Grove, Bibb County, by persons described as 'white incendiaries', reported in early July 1881. According to the same report, Black incendiaries burned the white church the next night, and the pairing of the two fires was the whole of the story as it circulated in newspaper news-summary columns.

episodes.title: Pursuit and shooting at Charles Harris near Leesburg, Georgia
episodes.lead: The pursuit and shooting at Charles Harris near Leesburg, Georgia, took place in early July 1881, when a member of a citizens' search party chased Harris, a Black railroad worker accused of assaulting a widow, and fired at him with a pistol. Harris returned fire, no one was hit, and he remained at large; the only report found, from the Albany Advertiser, called for his arrest for an "atrocious crime."

episodes.title: Shooting of Charles Parker
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The shooting of Charles Parker was the fatal wounding of an Adirondack guide by a constable in northern New York in August 1881, after Parker had been accused of assaulting a woman he was guiding and hunted by guides who threatened to lynch him. Parker escaped from custody, was shot by Constable Cole while being retaken at Long Lake, and died at Forked Lake days later. The case drew wide notice because the woman, Mrs. George Bull of Philadelphia, was bound for Senator Platt's camp, and because accounts of the shooting divided.

episodes.title: Cowan saw mill shooting
episodes.lead: The Cowan saw mill shooting was a confrontation at Cowan, Tennessee, reported in early August 1881, in which a railroad employee named Northcutt and other armed hands from his train fired on about thirty Black men gathered at a saw mill. The Black men fled and no one was reported hurt. The only known account, printed by the Winchester Home Journal as "The Cowan Affair," came from a local informant and presented the shooting as Northcutt's defense against a threatened attack.

episodes.title: Lynching of J. J. Dickison Jr.
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of J. J. Dickison Jr. was the killing of a prisoner in the jail at Leesburg, Sumter County, Florida, by a party of armed and disguised men at about 2 a.m. on Friday, July 15, 1881. Dickison, the son of a former Adjutant General of Florida, had been jailed the evening before, accused of shooting a Leesburg man named Beach with a shotgun. A coroner's jury attributed his death to unknown parties, and Florida editors widely condemned the killing, while the Leesburg paper argued that his record explained it.

episodes.title: Double Horn Mob attack on the Fall Creek camp meeting
episodes.lead: The Double Horn Mob attack on the Fall Creek camp meeting was the breaking up of a Methodist campmeeting on Fall creek, Texas, by about twenty men calling themselves the "Double Horn Mob" in late July 1881. The men cut saddles and stake ropes, threw rocks, fired pistols and beat a Black man who was asleep in a wagon on the grounds. An Austin Statesman correspondent reported it as a fresh "outrage" and urged that the men, several said to be known, be punished.

episodes.title: Lynching of Felix Wyley
episodes.lead: The lynching of Felix Wyley was the killing of a Black prisoner by a crowd at Tiptonville, Lake County, Tennessee, on a Monday night in late July 1881. Accused of raping and murdering a young white woman, Wyley was taken from the county jail after his preliminary hearing, hanged from a tree at the edge of town and shot. The wire story ran in papers across the country, and a month later Governor Hawkins offered a $5,000 reward for members of the mob.

episodes.title: Fernandina disturbance of July 1881
episodes.lead: The Fernandina disturbance of July 1881 was a street conflict in Fernandina, Florida, on July 4, 1881, in which a Black man was wounded during an arrest or a quarrel with a policeman's family, and a Black crowd then threatened the men held responsible. The mayor called out the local military and the governor sent troops from Jacksonville, and a wire brief carried the story to papers from New York to Dallas as a threatened riot.

episodes.title: Lynching of George C. O'Connor
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of George C. O'Connor was the hanging of the justice of the peace of Antonito, Colorado, by a vigilance committee on the night of July 21, 1881, though some reports place it a day later. The committee accused O'Connor of shielding and leading a gang of robbers, seized him in his saloon and hanged him in an old slaughter-house. Newspapers across the country carried the story as the hanging of a corrupt judge by 'Judge Lynch', most of them repeating the committee's charges as fact.

episodes.title: Whipping of Henry at Haynesville, Louisiana
episodes.lead: The whipping of Henry at Haynesville, Louisiana, took place on a Saturday night in mid-July 1881, when a man identified as young Mr. Smith whipped a Black boy named Henry, aged 15 or 16, and ordered him to leave. The only known account, a warning notice in an Arkansas weekly, accused Henry of entering Mrs. Smith's bedroom and urged readers to "look out for him."

episodes.title: Killing of Henry Allen
episodes.lead: The killing of Henry Allen took place on 5 July 1881 in a harvest field near Mount Sterling, Kentucky, where a Black farm worker named Allen had his throat cut by a man named Freeman. According to a Mount Sterling dispatch, a party came to Allen's house that night to lynch him on an accusation of assaulting a woman, but found him already dead.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Smith
episodes.lead: The lynching of Henry Smith took place in July 1881 at Des Arc, Arkansas, when thirty or forty men took the keys from the town's jailer and carried off Smith, a Black prisoner accused of raping and murdering a young orphan girl. They hanged him and threw his body into the river while townspeople followed and no one interfered. Wire briefs carried the story across the country, and Memphis papers openly endorsed the lynching.

episodes.title: Lynching of Houston Turner
episodes.lead: The lynching of Houston Turner took place on the night of July 18, 1881, in Murfreesboro, Tennessee, when a mob of about one hundred men took Turner, a nineteen-year-old Black man, from the Rutherford County sheriff and hanged him in the court-house yard. Turner had been accused of raping a white woman, Mary O'Neal, ten days earlier. The killing was reported nationally, defended by several Southern papers, and named in a reward proclamation by Governor Hawkins.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Howell Edmunds
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Howell Edmunds took place on the night of July 4, 1881, when five masked men tried to take Edmunds from the jail at Monticello, Drew County, Arkansas, where he was held on a charge of murdering his sister-in-law, Sallie Watson. Sheriff Hammock turned the men back, and Edmunds remained in jail while papers predicted that he would still be lynched. The case drew notice because the dead girl belonged to a prominent Drew County family, and the attempt was reported as far away as Chicago and Wisconsin.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Henry Lawson
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Henry Lawson took place in Chattanooga, Tennessee, in July 1881, when a mob gathered at night in front of the jail where Lawson, a Black man accused of raping and cutting a young woman, was being held. According to a Chattanooga telegram dated July 11, the men were deterred by a strong sheriff's guard. Lawson was later convicted in the circuit court at Chattanooga and sentenced to hang, and the case ran as brief items in Georgia, Tennessee and Louisiana papers.

episodes.title: South Baltimore Fourth of July brawl (1881)
episodes.lead: The South Baltimore Fourth of July brawl was a street fight between white and Black residents of South Baltimore, Maryland, on July 4, 1881, in which a white man, William Hecker, and a Black man, Isaac Curtis, were shot. Both men were reported fatally or mortally wounded, and a Black man, Thomas H. Ross, was arrested on the charge of shooting Hecker. Papers outside Baltimore carried the case as one of a series of holiday shootings in the city.

episodes.title: Lynching of Isaac Fisher
episodes.lead: The lynching of Isaac Fisher took place on Monday, July 25, 1881, when a crowd took Fisher, a Black blacksmith, from his guards at Satartia in Yazoo County, Mississippi, and hanged him from a tree outside the village. Fisher was accused of raping a young white woman and drowning her in a cistern two days earlier. Wire dispatches spread the case nationally under approving headlines.

episodes.title: Lynching of J. L. Jennings
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of J. L. Jennings was the hanging of Jennings, a farm hand accused of murder, after an armed band took him from the jail at Tierra Amarilla, the seat of Rio Arriba County, New Mexico Territory, on the night of July 23 or 24, 1881. Jennings had been arrested with Mrs. Lewis, the wife of his employer, after the body of the farmer Lewis was found buried near an irrigation ditch on the Animas River, and both were reported to have confessed. A two-line Santa Fe brief ran from California to Maine, and fuller accounts blamed a vigilance committee that thought the jail unsafe.

episodes.title: Shooting of Jack Hicks
episodes.lead: The shooting of Jack Hicks was the wounding of a Black man by a sheriff in South Carolina in late July or on 1 August 1881, as he ran from an attempted arrest. The sheriff fired four shots and hit Hicks twice, but Hicks escaped and was reported likely to die. The only account is a paragraph from the Williamsburg Herald, reprinted on 4 August in state-news columns in Anderson and Savannah.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of James Atkinson
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of James Atkinson was a rumor, carried by several newspapers in July 1881, that a man held in the jail at Gayoso, Pemiscot County, Missouri, on a charge of murdering his wife and infant child had been taken out at night and lynched. Later reports contradicted it: in late July and again in late August Atkinson was described as alive in the Gayoso jail, with his trial set for September.

episodes.title: St. Joseph exposition grounds riot (1881)
episodes.lead: The St. Joseph exposition grounds riot was an attack on Black people by a crowd of "roughs" at the exposition grounds in St. Joseph, Missouri, on July 4, 1881. The crowd tried to drive all "colored people" off the grounds, fractured one man's skull, beat a youth unconscious and fatally injured an old man named Harris before the military and extra police put down what the report called a riot.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Jim Offutt
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Jim Offutt took place at about 1 a.m. on a Friday in late July 1881, when a large body of masked men came to the jail in Paris, Bourbon County, Kentucky, and demanded Offutt, a prisoner accused of frightening a woman to death. The jailer escaped with the keys and raised an alarm, and the men withdrew when townspeople filled the streets. A Georgia paper cited the episode as one town's stand against lynch law, and Offutt was shot dead by his brother-in-law about three weeks later.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Smith (Laurens County, Georgia)
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Smith was the shooting of a Black man by a mob in Laurens County, Georgia, reported in late July 1881. Accused of attempting the outrage of Mrs. R. T. Downing, Smith was found asleep by a pursuing mob the next day and shot to death. The episode is known only from one short paragraph printed in two Ohio newspapers under the headline "An Easy Death."

episodes.title: Killing of Jordan Thompson
episodes.lead: The killing of Jordan Thompson was the shooting of a Black man by a pursuing party near Dresden, Tennessee, after he was accused of cutting a white man on Sunday, July 31, 1881. According to the widely reprinted Dresden dispatch, officers shot him dead when he refused to surrender, while one Pennsylvania digest attributed the killing to "the avengers of Prewett." Northern and Southern papers carried the news as a brief crime item over the following week.

episodes.title: Threats against Black railroad laborers in Crawford County, Indiana
episodes.lead: In late July 1881, Black laborers hired to build the Louisville, New Albany and St. Louis railroad in Crawford County, Indiana, were threatened with exclusion from the county, and local officials refused to protect them. Reports differed on whether construction halted or the men went to work, but no violence was reported. Papers in Indianapolis, Chicago, Memphis and Savannah carried the story, the Indianapolis Leader calling it "a gross outrage" in a state "north of the Ohio river."

episodes.title: Killing of Levi Bolden
episodes.lead: The killing of Levi Bolden took place on the morning of July 24, 1881, in the county jail at Paducah, Kentucky, where the jailer and county officials shot Bolden, a Black prisoner awaiting transfer to the penitentiary. According to the officers, Bolden had just beaten his cellmate John Stewart to death and attacked them when they opened the cell. A coroner's jury upheld the shooting the same day, and the story of the jail "tragedy" ran in papers across the country into August.

episodes.title: Lynching of Hicks Ross
episodes.lead: The lynching of Hicks Ross was the reported hanging of a Black prisoner by a mob that took him from the jail at Linden, Cass County, Texas, on Sunday, July 10, 1881. He had been jailed on the accusation of fatally cutting Dr. H. J. Avinger, a physician at Avinger Station on the East Line railroad. Word of the lynching came through the Dallas Herald, first as a rumor 'pretty well confirmed' and then as beyond 'little doubt'.

episodes.title: Mineral Springs courthouse standoff
episodes.lead: The Mineral Springs courthouse standoff was a confrontation on July 7, 1881, at Mineral Springs, Howard County, Arkansas, between a crowd of about 200 armed Black people at a trial and armed white men of the town who turned out to protect the court officers. No one was reported hurt, but a number of Black men, including the crowd's leader, were arrested. Papers across the country carried the story as a 'Negro Riot' or a 'Race Conflict'.

episodes.title: Mahanoy City threatened lynching of 1881
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Mahanoy City threatened lynching of 1881 was an incident in early July 1881 in which a crowd in Mahanoy City, Pennsylvania, went after a man accused of a remark approving of the attempt on President Garfield's life. One account said the crowd had a rope around his neck before letting him go, while another said he denied the remark and was left unharmed.

episodes.title: Lynching of Robert Barker
episodes.lead: The lynching of Robert Barker was the shooting of a Black prisoner by an armed group of Black men on the road from Okolona to Houston, in Chickasaw County, Mississippi, on July 30, 1881. Barker, accused of killing Luther White, a Black man, about three weeks earlier, was taken from an officer about five or six miles from Okolona, carried into the woods and shot dead. White papers headlined the case as a Black murderer "Lynched by a Mob of His Own Color," and the Okolona paper said the victim had received "a justly merited punishment."

episodes.title: Posse shooting of Scott Lanier's assailant
episodes.lead: The posse shooting of Scott Lanier's assailant took place in July 1881 in the "tenth ward" of a Louisiana parish, when a constable and posse pursued and shot an unnamed Black man accused of shooting Scott Lanier. First reported as "fatally wounded," the man was described three weeks later as alive after the amputation of an arm, while Lanier had recovered.

episodes.title: Lynching of Silas Lee
episodes.lead: The lynching of Silas Lee was the killing of a Black farm hand by a crowd in Lincoln parish, Louisiana, about seven miles from Vienna, in July 1881. Accused by his employer's wife of being found under her young daughter's bed, Lee was shot and left for dead, then taken out again two nights later and killed. A Baton Rouge paper printed the full account under the heading "JUDGE LYNCH" and openly approved of the killing.

episodes.title: Lynching of Spence
episodes.lead: The lynching of Spence was the hanging of a young Black man near Frog Level, Caddo Parish, Louisiana, in mid-July 1881. Spence, said to be about 18, was accused of trying to enter a girl's room at a local house and was later found hanged. A Shreveport paper approved the killing under the heading 'Quick Justice', and the item was reprinted in Louisiana and Tennessee.

episodes.title: Lynching of Frank Craft, William Underwood and James Butler
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Frank Craft, William Underwood and James Butler took place on the night of July 1, 1881, when a mob took the three men from the jail at Greenfield, Dade County, Missouri, and hanged them in the court-yard. The men were jailed as horse thieves and described as members of a gang led by Taylor Underwood, who was accused of killing the Greenfield officer McElrath. The hanging was reported in brief items across the country in July and was recalled in August when Taylor Underwood was arrested at Carthage.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Thomas Brayton
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Thomas Brayton was an armed attack by a mob on the house of a Black man at or near Paoli, Orange County, Indiana, on the night of Sunday, July 31, 1881. The defenders drove the attackers off with gunfire, and the mob withdrew carrying its wounded, with no one in the house reported hurt. An Indianapolis paper praised the armed defense as an example, while a wire brief carried the story to papers in the Dakotas and Minnesota.

episodes.title: Assault on William Tinker
episodes.lead: The assault on William Tinker was a knife attack on a Black bootblack by Samuel Frasier, a white man from Richmond, Virginia, at the St. James Hotel corner in Washington, D.C., on Saturday, July 2, 1881. Frasier said Tinker had cursed President Garfield; the Police Court fined him $5 or 15 days.

episodes.title: Lynching of Tom Stewart
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Tom Stewart was the hanging of a man accused of double murder by masked men who took him from his captor near Old Agency, on the Teton in Montana Territory, on the evening of July 1, 1881. Stewart, whom the Fort Benton River Press named Brackett E. Stewart, was accused of killing O. H. Morgan and Mrs. Annie Armstrong and burning their house two days earlier. A coroner's jury found him hanged by persons unknown, and the Montana papers presented the lynching as deserved punishment.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jesse Waldrop
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jesse Waldrop was the killing in early July 1881 of a 23-year-old man accused of raping and murdering a young bride, Mrs. Mitchell, by armed men who took him from a Georgia jail to the roadside spot where her body had been found. Early wire reports said he was hanged there, but a LaGrange correspondent and a Cincinnati Enquirer special said he was burned alive at a stake. Papers across the country told the story as deserved retribution, and two described Waldrop as white.

episodes.title: Lynching of Wash Allen
episodes.lead: The lynching of Wash Allen took place in DeSoto Parish, Louisiana, in July 1881, when thirty or forty masked men took Allen, a Black man jailed at Mansfield on suspicion of murdering the Kingston merchant M. J. (Judd) Scott, and hanged him at Kingston. Allen was reported to have confessed and named four or five other Black men, but a later Shreveport Times item said the confession was extorted and that the men he named proved an alibi. The hanging ran as a one-line wire item across the country, while a Mansfield correspondent wrote that local citizens approved it.

episodes.title: P Street shooting claim, Washington, 1881
episodes.lead: The P Street shooting claim was an account given in July 1881 by an unnamed Black man held at Police Headquarters in Washington, D.C., who said a crowd had tried to shoot him on P street for cheering for the President. No attack was confirmed, and the papers presented him as one of several "cranks" who had appeared at police headquarters.

episodes.title: Death of Wilson Calder
episodes.lead: The death of Wilson Calder was the death of a Black man on Edisto Island, South Carolina, on July 3, 1881, two days after he fought two white brothers, Marlon and Harry Seabrook. Black residents held that the fight killed him, a doctor found no marks of violence, and the dispute halted the inquest and left the body unburied about a week.

episodes.title: Hanging of a Black man in Helton Township, Ashe County
episodes.lead: The hanging of a Black man in Helton Township, Ashe County, was the killing of an unnamed Black man described as a "little negro dwarf" in northwestern North Carolina, reported in August 1881 as having taken place "not long since." He was hanged for allegedly stabbing a white girl, and the only report named the man who carried out the hanging as "a man by the name of Lynch."

episodes.title: Benson gambling den expulsion
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Benson gambling den expulsion was an 1881 incident in which the citizens of Benson, Arizona, burned the furniture of a gambling den and ordered its occupants to leave by the first train or be lynched, after a deputy sheriff was shot. The episode was known mainly through a one-sentence wire item that ran in Michigan, Wisconsin and Texas papers in September 1881, and none of the reports gave the race of anyone involved.

episodes.title: Lynching of the "Black Kid" in Silverton, Colorado
episodes.lead: The lynching of the "Black Kid" was the hanging of a young Black man by the Vigilance Committee of Silverton, Colorado, in late August 1881, after he was jailed in connection with the killing of the town's city marshal. Colorado papers called him the "Black Kid," while a Chicago Tribune correspondent named him Jim Catrin. Wire reports mentioned his death in a single sentence within the pursuit of the marshal's accused killers, one of whom, Burt Wilkinson, was later taken from the same jail and hanged.

episodes.title: Killing of four Mexican prisoners near Dolores, Texas
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The killing of four Mexican prisoners near Dolores, Texas, took place on August 25, 1881, when unknown attackers fired on four men accused of horse theft as their captors carried them toward the jail at Brackett. All four were killed, and an inquest returned a verdict that they had died at the hands of persons unknown. A wire dispatch carried the news across the country, where papers variously described it as "Summary Justice", a lynching and a murder.

episodes.title: Killing of Charles Dew
episodes.lead: The killing of Charles Dew was the murder of a Black farmer in Riley Township, Clinton County, Michigan, who was found beaten and hanged in his barn after the night of August 23, 1881. Weeks or months earlier a party of men had tarred and feathered him and threatened his life, and the killers were never identified in the coverage. Several Eastern papers carried the story under headlines calling it the work of Michigan "Kuklux".

episodes.title: Lynching of Charles Stewart
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Charles Stewart was the hanging of a Black man accused of murdering his wife, whom a mob took from the county jail at Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, about midnight on Monday, August 15, 1881. The local paper reported that the crowd demanding his death was made up of Black men and women, and a widely reprinted wire item said his father-in-law prayed for him and then helped hang him. The nearest newspaper condemned the lynching because Stewart had been awaiting trial in circuit court on circumstantial evidence.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Charles Stone
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Charles Stone took place at Mears, Colorado, in late August 1881, when armed men searched for Stone, a man suspected of killing a man named McCorkey, with the stated intention of lynching him. Officials who had arrested Stone moved him away from a group of the dead man's friends, and no report in the coverage shows that the searchers found or harmed him. A Denver News dispatch about the threat ran in papers from California to Maine, while a later letter from Mears identified the dead man as Edward McClarkey and did not mention a mob.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of a Chinese boy on Roberts Island
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of a Chinese boy on Roberts Island took place on August 23, 1881, when an 11-year-old Chinese boy accused of setting fire to a grain stack on a ranch near Stockton, California, was captured and tied by his cue to a header-wagon. According to the only dispatch on the case, he would have been hanged had women on the ranch not interfered, and he was instead arraigned in court at Stockton. The Sacramento Daily Record-Union reported it as a "Narrow Escape of a Chinese Incendiary from Lynching," and a Nevada paper reprinted the item.

episodes.title: Killing of Henry Cole
episodes.lead: The killing of Henry Cole was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Deputy Sheriff Cornelius of Issaquena County at Edwards, Mississippi, on a Tuesday shortly before 4 August 1881. Cornelius had come to arrest Cole and other men accused of leaving a labor contract, and after the shooting he was jailed and bound over to the Hinds County circuit court. A Mississippi paper reported that the shooting was regarded locally as "a great outrage."

episodes.title: Killing of Columbus Hill
episodes.lead: The killing of Columbus Hill was the fatal stabbing of a Black bootblack by Daniel Sullivan, a white man, opposite the Hanover Market in South Baltimore, Maryland, on the night of August 20, 1881. Police arrested Sullivan within minutes while a large Black crowd followed them threatening to lynch him, and a wire report of an "apparently unprovoked and wanton" killing ran from New York to Minnesota.

episodes.title: Beating of an unnamed Black man in Webster Parish, Louisiana (1881)
episodes.lead: The beating of an unnamed Black man in Webster Parish, Louisiana, took place in August 1881, when neighbors gave a man accused of attempting to outrage a Mrs. Crow 'a sound thrashing' and ordered him to leave the country. No death was reported, and the episode is known from a single paragraph in the Richland Beacon's column of Louisiana state news, whose editor wrote that the neighbors 'ought to have broken his neck.'

episodes.title: Shooting of Cuff (Henry Brooks) at Lake City
episodes.lead: The shooting of Cuff, alias Henry Brooks, took place at Lake City, Florida, on a Wednesday afternoon in August 1881, when a deputy sheriff and a man he had summoned fired on Brooks, a Black man, as he fled arrest. A pistol ball struck him in the back of the head without serious harm, and he was captured and held under a justice's warrant.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of David Lewis
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of David Lewis took place near Elberton, Georgia, on 10 August 1881, when a crowd of Black people tried to take Lewis, a white man, from his guard after he killed a Black man named Governor Harper with a hoe. The guard fired small shot into the crowd and later dispersed it, and Lewis was afterward bound over to the Superior Court for involuntary manslaughter.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of George Nickel
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of George Nickel took place at Brownsville, Pennsylvania, in August 1881, when neighbors of Dr. George Nickel threatened to lynch him for alleged cruelty to his young wife. Nickel left the town for "parts unknown" and was not harmed, and the episode survives only as a one-sentence item in Pennsylvania news columns.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Ed Anderson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Ed Anderson took place near Oakley and Madisonville, outside Cincinnati, Ohio, in August 1881, when residents hunting two Black men accused of highway robbery caught Anderson and nearly lynched him. His companion escaped after about a hundred shots were fired at him, and Anderson was held as a prisoner. The capture ran as a wire item from Utah to Arizona, while only an Ohio weekly reported the near-lynching.

episodes.title: Lynching of Ed Reeves
episodes.lead: The lynching of Ed Reeves was the killing of a Black man by a mob in Ballard County, Kentucky, in mid-August 1881, after he was accused of an attempted assault on a woman in Graves County. Captured in Ballard County, he was taken from the men bringing him to the Graves County jail and, by most accounts, hanged. The story reached papers from Pennsylvania to Georgia as a short wire item, headed in some of them 'A BRUTE LYNCHED'.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Frank Hudson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Frank Hudson took place in southwest Georgia in August 1881, when crowds sought to kill Hudson, a Black man accused of an axe murder in Terrell County, first at the jail in Albany and then at Dawson. At Dawson a crowd of 1,500 to 2,000 people took him to the court house intending to execute him, but local citizens persuaded it to let him be jailed. Hudson was later convicted and sentenced to hang, after a Chicago paper had reported that he had probably been lynched.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Fred Henderson
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Fred Henderson took place at Canton, Kansas, in August 1881, when a mob clamored to lynch Henderson, a Black man charged with attempted rape. Henderson was acquitted at his preliminary hearing and returned to Emporia, and the Emporia weekly news, which had first reported the charge as his offense, declared him innocent.

episodes.title: Crisfield riot (1881)
episodes.lead: The Crisfield riot was an outbreak of violence in Crisfield, Maryland, on August 19 and 20, 1881, in which white men beat a Black man named Tucker, a white man named George Holland was shot in Goodsell's Alley, and a white crowd the next night took over the alley and fired on its Black residents. An elderly Black man was wounded and no arrests were reported, though a reward of up to $500 was later offered. Accounts in the Snow Hill and Baltimore papers differed over how the shooting began.

episodes.title: Killing of Governor Harper
episodes.lead: The killing of Governor Harper was the death of a Black road hand, Governor Harper, struck on the head with a hoe by a white man, David Lewis, during a quarrel near Ruckersville, Georgia, in early August 1881. Lewis was arrested, and a crowd of Black men then tried to take him from his guard to lynch him.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of the Hardin brothers, Fredonia, Kansas
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of the Hardin brothers took place at the jail in Fredonia, Kansas, in the night of 7-8 August 1881, when about forty armed and masked men tried to seize two brothers held for murder. The attack failed after the mob's leader, a farmer named John Hoffman, was shot at the cell door and killed, and the rest of the attackers fled. Papers across the country ran the story as a case of lynchers foiled, and several editorials used it as a lesson against lynch law.

episodes.title: Lynching of William Epperson
episodes.lead: The lynching of William Epperson took place on August 13, 1881, near Abbeville in Vermilion Parish, Louisiana, when a crowd took him from the parish jail and hanged him. Epperson, a Black man, had been arrested that morning on the accusation that he murdered the wife and daughter of Pine Henderson, a Black resident of the parish. The local paper and the Baton Rouge press described the crowd as made up of both white and Black men and presented the hanging as deserved punishment.

episodes.title: Killing of Henry Foster
episodes.lead: The killing of Henry Foster was the shooting of a Black farmer who was called out of his house at night near Covington, Tennessee, in August 1881 and shot dead. The assassin escaped, and the case reached newspapers only as a one-sentence wire item from Memphis.

episodes.title: Killing of a Black prisoner near Horn Lake, Mississippi
episodes.lead: The killing of a Black prisoner near Horn Lake, Mississippi, took place in late August 1881, when four or five armed men stopped a marshal taking an unnamed Black man to jail at Hernando, ordered the marshal away and shot the prisoner dead on the road. The Memphis Daily Appeal reported it as a murder, and no arrests were reported.

episodes.title: Lynching of Joe Caleb
episodes.lead: The lynching of Joe Caleb took place on the night of August 31, 1881, when a party of armed men took Caleb, a young Black man held on a charge of attempting to burn a house, from the jail at Vernon in Jackson Parish, Louisiana, and hanged him beside the Trenton road. Caleb had been accused of setting fire to the house of T. J. Fuller the previous April while thirteen people were inside. An inquest failed to identify the lynchers, and a New Orleans Item editorial said it could "hardly blame" them.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Edward Johnson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Edward Johnson took place in Emporia, Kansas, on the evening of August 5, 1881, when a crowd of a hundred to three hundred men gathered at the Lyon county jail to hang Johnson, a Black man accused of killing Deputy Sheriff James Spillman. Johnson escaped harm because Sheriff Moon had already sent him under guard to Cottonwood Falls, and he was later committed to the asylum at Ossawatomie. The Emporia Weekly News condemned the gathering as mob law that would have disgraced the town and praised the sheriff for averting it.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Juan Morales
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Juan Morales took place on August 14, 1881, when a group of would-be lynchers pursued Morales, accused of a fatal shooting at Tempe, Arizona Territory, as a constable rode with him to the jail at Phoenix. The constable lodged Morales in jail a few minutes before the pursuers arrived, and Morales was later bound over to the grand jury. A Phoenix telegram carried the story to Pacific Coast dailies as a 'Narrow Escape from Lynching'; the local press reported the man killed and the accused both as Mexicans.

episodes.title: Shooting at Samuel R. Hurst
episodes.lead: The shooting at Samuel R. Hurst was an attack at Laredo, Texas, in late summer 1881 in which unidentified assailants fired three or four times at Hurst, a Black man recently appointed inspector, or river guard, on the Rio Grande. He was not reported hurt, and the papers that carried the story tied the attack to his color.

episodes.title: Lynching of Levi Smith
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Levi Smith was the hanging of a young man from Crawford County, Indiana, by a mob near Buleyville, Harrison County, Kentucky, in late August 1881. Smith was accused of killing a man and fleeing, and the mob pursued and hanged him. Indiana sources presented him as a "desperado" with a record of violence, and the story ran mainly as a brief item in Midwestern crime roundups.

episodes.title: Killing of Lovels Green and Mrs. Alguire
episodes.lead: The killing of Lovels Green and Mrs. Alguire was a double homicide at Grand Haven, Michigan, on the night of about August 14, 1881, in which John Allguire shot Green, a Black man who had lived for several years with Allguire's white mother, and his mother also died. Allguire surrendered and claimed self-defence, but a coroner's jury found that he had killed both. Newspapers from New York to Virginia carried the story, stressing that the dead man was 'colored' and the woman white.

episodes.title: Killing of Mack Allen
episodes.lead: The killing of Mack Allen was the fatal shooting of a Black man, named as Mack Allen or McAllen, by Jerome Pasley and a party of neighborhood men in Grayson County, Virginia, near the North Carolina line, in mid-August 1881. Allen was accused of attempting an "outrage" on a young girl, and both accounts say he was shot dead after he fired a pistol at Pasley, who was trying to take him. Both surviving accounts give the pursuers' version, and a short Virginia news paragraph about the case was reprinted in Delaware, Washington and West Virginia.

episodes.title: Whipping death of a Mexican boy in Ramsey's Canyon
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The whipping death of a Mexican boy in Ramsey's Canyon took place about August 21, 1881, when a mob of about a dozen men in the Huachuca Mountains near Tombstone, Arizona Territory, forced Mexican woodcutters to flog a boy accused of insulting a girl. The boy was reported to have died of the beating, and the girl afterward said she had invented the story "for fun." The wire account ran in papers across the country, and the girl's father was arrested and examined before a magistrate at Charleston.

episodes.title: White laborers' protest against Black workers on the New York, Ontario and Western Railroad
episodes.lead: The white laborers' protest against Black workers on the New York, Ontario and Western Railroad was a labor dispute in Orange County, New York, in August 1881, when Irish and Italian laborers grading the new line threatened to strike over reports that contractors were bringing Black workers from Maryland and the District of Columbia at $1.25 a day. New York and Chicago papers warned of a strike or riot and a protest meeting at Middletown, while correspondents writing from Middletown called the reports exaggerated. No violence was reported, and by August 9 the New-York Tribune declared the trouble over after the contractors disclaimed any present plan to bring more Black workers.

episodes.title: Lynching of Mike Wells
episodes.lead: The lynching of Mike Wells was the hanging of a Black man by a mob in the Court House yard at Dyersburg, Dyer County, Tennessee, on August 1, 1881. Wells had been arrested on an accusation of attempting to outrage a widow, Mrs. Childs, and was said to have confessed before the mob took him from his guard. The wire report ran in papers across the country, and later that month Governor Hawkins offered a $5,000 reward for the conviction of the men who had mobbed him.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of a waiter at Mont Eagle
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of a waiter at Mont Eagle was a night attack in early August 1881 in which a mob of a dozen or more young men broke into the quarters of the Black waiters at a hotel in Mont Eagle, Tennessee, to lynch one of them. The waiter escaped when he was locked in a hotel room, and the mob's members were arrested and released on their promises not to repeat the act. The Memphis Public Ledger reported it as a "genuine sensation" under the headline "A colored Waiter That Barely Escaped Lynching."

episodes.title: Morrilton racial disturbance (1881)
episodes.lead: The Morrilton racial disturbance was a period of racial conflict in Morrilton, Arkansas, in August 1881, after a white parent beat a Black man accused of abusing white children. Street fights followed between supporters of both sides, officers swore in special police, and townspeople asked the governor for a military company. Wire reports carried it nationally as a looming "war of races," while the Conway County sheriff wrote that no such conflict was expected.

episodes.title: Shooting of a Black man by a New Orleans policeman (1881)
episodes.lead: In August 1881 a New Orleans policeman named Reishe shot an unnamed Black man through the breast. The officer said the shooting was accidental, and a brief report in a Covington weekly added that he "will be promoted."

episodes.title: Lynching of Alex Wilson and Perry Munson
episodes.lead: The lynching of Alex Wilson and Perry Munson took place at Monroe, Louisiana, on the night of August 22-23, 1881, when a mob took the two Black prisoners from the parish jail and hanged them outside town. Both men were held on charges of murdering other Black men and had not been tried. The Monroe papers condemned the killing, and a New Orleans Democrat dispatch carried brief notices of it nationally.

episodes.title: Pocomoke City disturbance of 1881
episodes.lead: The Pocomoke City disturbance of 1881 was a confrontation between white youths and Black men in Pocomoke City, Worcester County, Maryland, beginning on Saturday evening, August 27, 1881. After a Black man was knocked down and the youths reportedly threatened to drive Black residents out, 50 or 60 Black men paraded the streets two nights later. Writs followed for 52 of the Black men, and the Snow Hill Democratic Messenger dismissed reports of a "riot" as exaggerated.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching near Pine Grove, Pennsylvania (1881)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching near Pine Grove was the capture and threatened lynching of an unnamed man by a pursuing party in the woods near Pine Grove, apparently in Pennsylvania, reported in August 1881. The man, accused of attacking a young woman on Scalp's Mountain north of Port Clinton, was spared after he pleaded for mercy and was sent to jail. The only report found does not give his race.

episodes.title: Queenstown lynching threats
episodes.lead: The Queenstown lynching threats were threats in August 1881 to lynch Black suspects in the killing of two children, Joseph and Lizzie Fisher, at Queenstown in the county outside Washington, D.C. Early dispatches said men at a Washington market talked of lynching a missing Black farm hand, while the local investigation turned to an elderly Black woman, Christina Taylor, whom police later hurried to jail ahead of would-be lynchers. No lynching is reported, and the murder itself was called one of the most shocking crimes in the area in years.

episodes.title: Orange, Texas, lynchings of 1881
episodes.lead: The Orange, Texas, lynchings of 1881 were the killings of several Black men by armed white citizens of Orange, Texas, on August 17-21, 1881, after Sheriff George W. Michael was shot pursuing Sam Saxon and others. Robert Saxon was hanged from an oak in town, others were shot, and on August 21 an armed party took Sam Saxon and another prisoner from the jail and shot them. Reported deaths ranged from three to eight, and the killings drew national wire coverage and a protest by Black residents of Galveston.

episodes.title: Shooting of an escaping prisoner in Savannah (1881)
episodes.lead: The shooting of an escaping prisoner in Savannah took place on the evening of 26 August 1881, when an officer taking an unnamed Black man to jail fired at him as he ran and hit him in the thigh. The wounded man was recaptured and returned to the jail, and the Savannah Morning News reported the incident in a brief local item the next morning.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of "Shorty" and "Reddy" at McKeesport
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of "Shorty" and "Reddy" took place at McKeesport, Pennsylvania, in August 1881, when a crowd gathered around the borough jail and threatened to lynch two men held as suspected leaders of the gang that had killed merchant George A. McClure. No attack on the jail was reported, and a later item said the two men jailed at McKeesport had no connection with the gang and would be released. The episode reached papers from Maine to Georgia as part of national wire coverage of the McKeesport manhunt.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Al Howe and Tom Benway
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Al Howe and Tom Benway took place at Sun River Crossing, Montana Territory, on the night of August 29, 1881, when four men put ropes around the necks of the two young men to force them to confess to stealing money. Both survived, and four men were bound over to the grand jury on a charge of attempting to hang them. The Benton Weekly Record condemned the affair as an outrage, and a Sun River correspondent of the Rocky Mountain Husbandman mocked it as an "amateur hanging bee."

episodes.title: Lynching of Thomas James Noakes
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Thomas James Noakes took place early on August 7, 1881, when masked and armed men took him from the jail at Oroville, Butte County, California, and hanged him from an oak tree on the road to Chico. Noakes was being held for the killing of A. J. Crum at Chico about three weeks earlier. A coroner's jury found that he died by mob violence and named no one, and the case drew opposing editorials in California and Nevada papers.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Tom Orchard and Wm. Tivris at Grain Valley
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Tom Orchard and Wm. Tivris was an incident at Grain Valley, Jackson County, Missouri, shortly before 6 August 1881, in which a posse of citizens captured two men accused of the "inhuman treatment" of a woman, and the men "narrowly escaped lynching." They were jailed at Independence instead, and the case appeared only as a short item in a Missouri news column.

episodes.title: Clubbing of Tom Wilson
episodes.lead: The clubbing of Tom Wilson was a police beating in Wadesboro, North Carolina, in about early August 1881, when two town policemen knocked Wilson, a Black man, senseless with their clubs while arresting him. A crowd of Black residents then rushed the officers, and the sheriff, the town marshal and a judge intervened; the only surviving report presented the affair as an "ugly sequel" to a political speech.

episodes.title: False River ball shooting
episodes.lead: The False River ball shooting was an exchange of gunfire at a Black ball on False River, Pointe Coupee Parish, Louisiana, near midnight on August 13, 1881, in which a white man, L. T. Chenvert, was killed, a white youth, Joseph Garon, was wounded, and several Black men were wounded by shotgun fire. Sixteen Black men were jailed, and two, Val Dorval and Leopold Polite, were held for murder. Every account traces to the local Pointe Coupee Banner or to brief wire dispatches, which blamed the Black men under headlines such as "Murderous Negroes."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Voscamp
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Voscamp was a near-lynching in Michigan in which a man said to have murdered Lyman Cady near Coopersville 'narrowly escaped lynching by an infuriated gang of Cady's neighbors.' The episode was reported in late August 1881, when he was taken to Grand Rapids for safe-keeping. It survives only as one sentence in a syndicated column of state news.

episodes.title: Killing of William Jones (Nashville, 1881)
episodes.lead: The killing of William Jones was the fatal shooting of a Black man by James Ross, a white man, at Ross's house in Nashville, Tennessee, on Sunday, August 7, 1881. By the account sent over the wires, Jones had gone to ask Ross why he had hit a Black boy with a stone, and Ross answered by fetching a pistol and shooting him dead. The story ran as a short item in crime roundups across the country, while a Memphis paper printed a version in which Jones struck Ross first.

episodes.title: Center Point riots (1881)
episodes.lead: The Center Point riots were a series of armed clashes between Black and white men at Center Point, Howard County, Arkansas, in late August 1881. Dispatches from Little Rock reported that Black men, and in one account a white man, were killed, though they disagreed on the toll. The fullest account traced one battle to the beating of a Black man, Anderson Smith, by two white men, and the story ran in weekly papers across the Midwest.

episodes.title: Lynching of Sandy Wright
episodes.lead: The lynching of Sandy Wright was the shooting of a Black prisoner in the jail at Blakely, Early County, Georgia, by a party of masked men in late September 1881. Wright, whose first name was also printed as "Zandy" and "Andy," was serving a sentence for hog stealing when about a dozen men forced the jailer to surrender his key and killed him in his cell.
