The men were not identified, and the story spread from Georgia papers to a Chicago Tribune dispatch and editorial and to short items in weeklies across the country.

episodes.title: Lynching of Archie Walker
episodes.lead: The lynching of Archie Walker was the hanging of a Black man by "the citizens of Waco," Mississippi, reported in late September 1881. Walker was accused of attempting to "outrage" the daughter of a man identified as Capt. Lee, and he was hanged to a tree. The episode is known from a single one-sentence telegraphic item.

episodes.title: Atlanta Garfield memorial riot
episodes.lead: The Atlanta Garfield memorial riot was a clash on September 26, 1881, in which police, U.S. Fifth Artillery soldiers and white citizens clubbed and wounded Black people outside DeGive's Opera House in Atlanta, Georgia, during memorial services for President Garfield. Police arrested a dozen to twenty Black men, and a crowd that tried to rescue them was charged and dispersed. Papers reported it as a riot that disgraced a funeral occasion, and they disagreed on its cause and on whether anyone died.

episodes.title: Hanging of Whit Brown
episodes.lead: The hanging of Whit Brown was the reported hanging, in 1881, of a Black man accused of murder by people around Red Bluff, about thirty miles below Little Rock. First rumored as a lynching, it was then described by the Russellville Democrat as a hanging done only to make Brown reveal details of the crime, and his fate was not reported.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at Danville, Arkansas
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching at Danville, Arkansas, was a failed attempt by a mob in early September 1881 to break into the Yell County jail at Danville and hang three prisoners accused of murder, named in the reports as Bruce, Taylor and Burris. Warned in advance, the sheriff chained the prisoners together and hid them in the woods overnight while the mob searched for them in vain. The episode was reported chiefly as a prelude to what followed two days later, when a mob took Taylor and Bruce from the jail at Dardanelle and hanged them.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bert Wilkinson
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Bert Wilkinson took place in Silverton, Colorado, on the evening of Sunday, September 4, 1881, when a party of masked men overpowered the guards at the town jail and hanged him. Wilkinson was accused of killing Silverton's city marshal about ten days earlier, and his Black companion, Jim Catrin, had already been lynched from the same jail. Papers across the country noted the case for Wilkinson's composure on the gallows, his betrayal by the outlaw Ike Stockton, and his respectable Indiana family.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Elijah Church
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Elijah Church took place on a Sunday night in September 1881, when a crowd of about fifty people entered the jail at Taylorsville, Alexander County, North Carolina, intending to hang Church, who was accused of murdering Miss Caroline Thompson during a robbery. The crowd gave up after R. Z. Linney urged it to let the law take its course. Church was then moved to the jail at Newton for safety, and in early October a mob took him from that jail and hanged him.

episodes.title: Lynching of Donaldson (1881)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Donaldson was the hanging of a man described as a "desperado," whom a mob took out of the jail at a town printed as "Dainfield" in 1881. The only known report, a brief editorial item in the Brenham Weekly Banner of September 15, 1881, gave no date, charge or race for the victim. The item drew notice for a local correspondent's claim that the town's people regretted the violence, which the Banner answered with skepticism.

episodes.title: Lynching of Frank Luck
episodes.lead: The lynching of Frank Luck was the hanging of a Black man by a mob after he was taken from the city prison at Wortham, Texas, on a Thursday night in mid-September 1881. The news spread as a one-sentence wire item through papers in Washington, New York and Savannah. An inquest jury later could not fix the blame on anyone, which a Texas paper cited as proof that the law could not find lynchers.

episodes.title: Shooting of Hawthorne
episodes.lead: The shooting of Hawthorne took place in early September 1881 in Boon township, Columbia County, Arkansas, when men deputized to arrest Hawthorne, a Black man accused of stealing corn, shot him with buckshot and squirrel shot as he fled. He survived and was held in the county jail to await the grand jury. The only known report is a short local item in the Magnolia Columbia Banner.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Allen
episodes.lead: The lynching of Henry Allen was the hanging of a Black prisoner by a masked mob that broke into the jail at Jacksonport, Arkansas, at about two o'clock on the morning of September 10, 1881. Allen, whom a Chicago dispatch called Henry Wallace, had been jailed on a charge of stabbing a white saloon keeper in nearby Newport. The mob overpowered the jailor and the sheriff, and Arkansas papers condemned the lynching, which a Chicago dispatch called "premature" because the wounded man recovered.

episodes.title: Rushford lynching threat against Jacob Pruchker
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Rushford lynching threat against Jacob Pruchker took place in September 1881 near Rushford, Fillmore County, Minnesota, after a "Bohemian boy" was accused of shooting dead a farmer's daughter, Anna Martin. A search party captured him at his home before dawn and threatened him until he confessed, and threats to lynch him followed while he was held in custody. No harm to him was reported, and the papers treated the case mainly as a murder without motive.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Jacob Whitmore
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Jacob Whitmore occurred at Bellefontaine, Ohio, in early October 1881, when crowds gathered to hang Whitmore, a young farmer jailed on the charge of poisoning his wife. Sheriff H. M. Cline took him to a neighboring county before the crowd could act, and militia guarded the jail through the night. Whitmore was later indicted for first-degree murder; no paper gives the race of anyone involved.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jane Campbell
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jane Campbell was the burning of a Black woman at a stake by a mob near Dyke's Mill, Louisiana, in mid-September 1881. Campbell was accused of killing her two children, and after a coroner's jury blamed her for their deaths a mob of whites and blacks seized her and burned her alive. A Little Rock dispatch carried the story across the country, calling the crime and the punishment without parallel.

episodes.title: Killing of James Hawkins
episodes.lead: The killing of James Hawkins was the fatal shooting of a Black striker by New Orleans Police Sergeant Reynolds on the morning of September 10, 1881, during a strike of the city's cotton laborers. Hawkins, a member of the Cotton Teamsters' Association, was shot during an attempted arrest of strikers who had interfered with teamsters hauling cotton. His death led the mayor to call for troops and produced a funeral that a press dispatch called the largest in the city since the war, attended by white and Black labor organizations.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Joe Edwards
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Joe Edwards took place in St. Louis, Missouri, on the afternoon of September 13, 1881, when a street crowd seized Edwards, a Black steamboat fireman, after he fired a pistol in a quarrel with another Black man and wounded a woman passing by. The crowd held him while men ran for a rope, but police arrived and took him to the station. Telegraph dispatches carried the story to dailies in Texas, Tennessee, Indiana and Minnesota the next day, and Midwestern weeklies reprinted it in their crime roundups.

episodes.title: Mob hanging of John Russell near Saltillo, Indiana
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The mob hanging of John Russell took place near Saltillo, Indiana, on Friday, about 2 September 1881, when a man arrested on a charge of stealing a watch was taken from an officer and hanged up three times to make him confess. Russell survived after being revived with difficulty, and he protested his innocence throughout. The episode is known only from a one-paragraph wire brief reprinted in several daily papers; no local Indiana report was found.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Taylor and J. T. Bruce
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Taylor and J. T. Bruce took place on the night of Saturday, September 10, 1881, at Dardanelle, Yell County, Arkansas, when an armed mob took the two men, both charged with murder, from the town jail and hanged them from a tree nearby. A Little Rock dispatch carried the story nationally and said public opinion was with the lynchers, while an Arkansas weekly condemned the act and blamed slow courts for it.

episodes.title: Killing of Josephus Fairchild
episodes.lead: The killing of Josephus Fairchild took place on September 13, 1881, in Lake Charles, Louisiana, when deputy sheriffs shot a Black prisoner who broke from their custody minutes after he was sentenced to death for murder. Struck in the head by a deputy's rifle ball, he died in the parish jail that night, and a coroner's jury found the officers justified. Both Lake Charles weeklies described the escape at length, and the story ran across the country as a wire brief and as a reprinted narrative titled "A Race for Life".

episodes.title: Napier Iron Works attack
episodes.lead: The Napier Iron Works attack was a night assault in September 1881 by discharged white laborers on Black workers who had been hired in their place at the Napier Iron Works in Lawrence County, Tennessee. Accounts differed on its outcome: a Nashville report said a masked party severely beat a number of Black men, while another brief said the Black workers, who were armed, drove their attackers away. Tennessee papers described the conflict as a riot and a war between white and Black employees, and one brief called it a "race war."

episodes.title: Lynching of Frank and John McDonald
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Frank and John McDonald took place at Menominee, Michigan, on the night of September 27, 1881, when a mob broke into the county jail and killed the two men, who were held on a charge of stabbing two brothers named Kittson. A crowd that a Menominee dispatch put at over 500 people, "composed mostly of Frenchmen, Indians and half-breeds," dragged the prisoners through the street and hung their bodies from a tree beside the house where the quarrel had begun. Most papers carried only a brief wire item datelined Oconto, Wisconsin, which garbled the names and in some copies put the jail at Oconto.

episodes.title: Lynching of Frank and John McDonald
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Frank and John McDonald was the killing of two cousins by a mob at Menominee, Michigan, on the night of September 27, 1881, after they had been jailed on a charge of fatally stabbing a young man named Willie Kittson. A crowd that reports put at 400 to more than 500 people overpowered the sheriff, broke into the county jail and dragged the two men to their deaths. Wire summaries carried the story across the country in early October, and a Wisconsin paper later reported the arrest of members of the lynching party.

episodes.title: Police shooting of Miggs Tilford
episodes.lead: The police shooting of Miggs Tilford took place at Harrodsburg, Kentucky, in September 1881 or shortly before, when policeman Meisburg shot Tilford, a Black man, during an arrest. Tilford was severely wounded, and the only known report gave as the reason that he had resisted arrest.

episodes.title: Uniontown camp meeting shooting
episodes.lead: The Uniontown camp meeting shooting was a fight on Sunday, September 4, 1881, in which white "roughs" attacked Black attendees of a colored camp meeting near Uniontown, Fayette County, Pennsylvania. Thomas Gilbert, a Black man, was shot and thought fatally wounded, several others were shot or cut, and one Black man was chased four miles and shot in the back.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at Hot Springs, Arkansas (1881)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching at Hot Springs, Arkansas, was a failed attempt by armed, masked white men to break into the Hot Springs jail on the night of September 9-10, 1881, and lynch a Black prisoner charged with attempting to outrage an elderly woman, Mrs. J. Parker. The attackers were driven off by gunfire from the jail guards and from Black men who had gathered nearby, and the accounts differed on whether anyone was hurt. A month later, dispatches reported that a Black boy supposed to be the accused, who had escaped, was found dead near Malvern and "must have" been lynched by a pursuing posse. The case drew notice because Black residents armed themselves to defend the prisoner, which a Chicago Tribune dispatch said caused "intense indignation."

episodes.title: New Hope posse shooting
episodes.lead: The New Hope posse shooting was the killing of an unnamed Black man by a bailiff named Dennis at New Hope, Georgia, on September 1, 1881, while Dennis and a posse were trying to arrest a different man. According to the wire report, the man who was shot ran out of a hut the posse had come to search and proved not to be the man they were after. Papers across the country carried the item as a short curiosity under headlines such as "Shot the Wrong Man" and "An Unlucky Negro."

episodes.title: Reported lynching near Orchard Hill, Georgia
episodes.lead: The reported lynching near Orchard Hill, Georgia, was the hanging by a mob of an unnamed Black man accused of assaulting a white woman near Orchard Hill on September 12, 1881. The hanging appears in only one report, a telegraphic brief in the Washington National Republican; other printings of the same Atlanta dispatch said only that the man had been arrested and identified.

episodes.title: Lynching of Alexander Harris and Sam Bell
episodes.lead: The lynching of Alexander Harris and Sam Bell was the shooting of two Black men by lynchers in Milam County, Texas, on a Sunday night in September 1881, while they were being taken to jail. The two men were accused of murdering W. B. Davidson, a planter they worked for, and the one known report said their bodies were "riddled with bullets."

episodes.title: Lynching of Samuel Ramey
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Samuel Ramey was the hanging of a prisoner taken from the jail at Owingsville, Kentucky, by a band of masked men on the night of September 11, 1881. Ramey had been jailed for the killing of a young farmer, John Smith, a few days earlier. A brief Louisville wire carried the story to papers across the country within two days, and later Owingsville dispatches added that some thirty masked horsemen had done it.

episodes.title: Savannah railroad bridge clash (1881)
episodes.lead: The Savannah railroad bridge clash was a confrontation on the morning of September 22, 1881, in Savannah, Georgia, in which police charged a crowd of Black strikers who had rushed a train bringing replacement laborers. Five Black men were wounded, none seriously according to the wire report, and one of them, Wm. Williams, was shot in the leg. The clash drew notice because a dispatch carried in Northern papers reported eight men killed, a figure the Savannah and wire accounts do not support.

episodes.title: Savannah wharf strike shooting
episodes.lead: The Savannah wharf strike shooting was a confrontation on September 19, 1881, at the railroad bridge leading to the Central Railroad wharves in Savannah, Georgia, in which police sergeant H. H. Harvey was shot by someone in a crowd of Black striking laborers and police fired into the crowd. A squad of police with muskets then drove the strikers from the bridge, and no casualties among the crowd were confirmed. Harvey died of the wound a month later, and the strike brought out the city's militia.

episodes.title: Webb City saloon stabbings
episodes.lead: The Webb City saloon stabbings were a knife attack on two Black men, Thomas Bettes and Mack Richardson, by two white men, Berry Harwood and George Hughes, in a saloon at Webb City, Arkansas, on the night of Saturday, September 24, 1881. Bettes died within a few hours and Richardson was stabbed in the breast; Harwood was captured while Hughes escaped. A Little Rock dispatch calling it 'a horrible butchery' was reprinted across the country, and the Chicago Tribune described the killings as 'entirely unprovoked'.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Jeff D. Gillenwaters
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Jeff D. Gillenwaters took place on the night of September 9-10, 1881, when a masked mob took him from the jail at Senatobia, Tate County, Mississippi, where he was held on a charge of murder, and shot him several times outside town. First reports said he would not live, but he survived, named his attackers, and six men were arrested and held without bail. Papers noted the case chiefly because the intended victim lived to identify the lynchers.

episodes.title: Killing of Wm. Bowie
episodes.lead: The killing of Wm. Bowie was the fatal shooting of a Black steamboat roustabout by Shreveport, Louisiana, policeman E. C. McRady in late September or early October 1881, after Bowie was accused of shooting Aaron White, a Black man helping the officer make an arrest. According to the Shreveport Standard, McRady fired his rifle when Bowie advanced on him with a cocked pistol and refused to drop it. Louisiana state-news columns called Bowie a "colored desperado" and reported that McRady had been "exonerated from blame."

episodes.title: Lynching of Archie Wright
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Archie Wright was the reported killing of a man named Archie Wright at Vicksburg, Mississippi, in or shortly before early October 1881. He was said to have been lynched for "offering indignities to respectable young ladies," and the event is known only from a one-line news brief.

episodes.title: Lynching of Ben Robertson
episodes.lead: The lynching of Ben Robertson took place in the town of Jeanerette, Louisiana, in late September or early October 1881, when a group of armed men took Robertson, a Black man jailed on a charge of chicken stealing, out of the town jail at night, flogged him and killed him. Early reports said he was hanged, but the paper that first said so later corrected itself to say he was shot while running away. Three men were charged with his murder and held on bond, and Louisiana editors condemned the killing as mob law.

episodes.title: Pensacola and Atlantic Railroad camp shooting (1881)
episodes.lead: The Pensacola and Atlantic Railroad camp shooting was a night shooting in late October 1881 at Mr. English Albert's railroad camp in Florida that killed a colored man from Georgia and slightly wounded three others. It followed a quarrel between a white man named Turnage and a Black worker, and the two surviving reports disagree on who fired.

episodes.title: Lynching of Charles Jones
episodes.lead: The lynching of Charles Jones took place at Spadra, Johnson County, Arkansas, on Monday, October 31, 1881, when a mob took Jones, a Black man accused of attempting to rape a white woman, from an officer at the railroad depot and hanged him to a tree. Jones was hanged within twenty minutes of arriving at Spadra, after what the wire called a "short informal examination by a jury." A Little Rock dispatch carried the story across the country, where papers ran it under headlines such as "Speedy Justice" and "Judge Lynch's Court in Arkansas."

episodes.title: Lynching of Charles Pierce
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Charles Pierce took place on the night of October 1, 1881, in Bloomington, Illinois, when a crowd reported at 4,000 to 5,000 broke into the McLean County jail and hanged Pierce from a tree near the jail. Pierce, a young prisoner held for horse theft, was accused of shooting jailer Ted Franks to death a few hours earlier. Papers across the country noted that leading citizens had joined the mob, and editors later cited the case in debates over lynching in the North and the South.

episodes.title: Lynching of Elijah Church
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Elijah Church took place on the night of October 6, 1881, when a body of men took Church, a white prisoner, from the jail at Newton, Catawba County, North Carolina, and hanged him to a tree outside the town. Church was awaiting trial on a charge of murdering a Miss Thompson in Alexander County that August. A wire dispatch carried the news to papers across the country, and North Carolina reports tied the lynching to the confession of a second accused man, E. H. Dockery.

episodes.title: Lynching of Clark and Bardeau
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Clark and Bardeau was the hanging of two accused robbers, known as Clark, alias "Butch", and "Frenchy" Bardeau, from a cottonwood tree in Socorro, New Mexico Territory, on the night of 6 October 1881. Arrested on suspicion of robbing a store at Lamy, the two were taken from guard by a "committee" and left hanging under a placard reading "The fate of footpads and horse thieves." The story ran in papers across the country, and within weeks territorial papers cited it in complaints about mob rule at Socorro.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Daniel Wolfe
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Daniel Wolfe was an attack by a crowd on a prisoner at Urbana, Illinois, in late October 1881, in which Wolfe was dragged from an officers' wagon with a rope around his neck. Officers cut the rope and lodged him in jail, and the only account of the episode, carried by the Dallas Herald, does not give his race.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of Dick Ellison
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of Dick Ellison was the death of a Black youth found dead between Hot Springs and Malvern, Arkansas, in October 1881, as reported in a dispatch dated October 14. The dispatch supposed that the dead youth was Dick Ellison, accused of attempting to outrage Mrs. Jacob Parker, and concluded that he had been caught and lynched by a pursuing posse. The item ran in at least seven newspapers within two days, but the identification and the lynching both rested on inference.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Ed Partridge
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Ed Partridge followed the death of his six-year-old stepdaughter, Bell Holmes, on a Georgia plantation near Americus in late October or early November 1881. A coroner's jury found that the girl died of beatings at Partridge's hands, and he escaped from custody before a New York wire dispatch reported that local citizens threatened to lynch him. No lynching or recapture appears in the coverage, which spread the case nationally as a brief item under headlines such as "A Georgia Brute."

episodes.title: Lynching of Edmund Davis
episodes.lead: The lynching of Edmund Davis was the hanging of a Black man by a crowd of about 300 men near Heath's store in Union County, North Carolina, on the morning of Monday, October 17, 1881. Davis, accused of raping the daughter of an aged white widow, was taken from the constable's guard escorting him to jail and hanged near the scene of the alleged crime. Papers in both Carolinas reported that about a third of the crowd was Black and that some of them urged that he be burned.

episodes.title: Lynching of Elias Robertson
episodes.lead: The lynching of Elias Robertson was the hanging of a nineteen-year-old Black man by a crowd of 300 to 400 people at Morgan's Fork, Franklin County, Mississippi, on or shortly before October 9, 1881. Robertson was accused of assaulting an elderly white widow, Mrs. Ellen Johnson, and the crowd, described as both Black and white, decided his fate by a vote before hanging him in daylight. Newspapers that carried the story stressed the vote and the crowd's mixed racial makeup, under headlines such as "Lynched by Popular Vote" and "The Voice of the Majority."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Fayette Hardee
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Fayette Hardee took place at Vaiden, Mississippi, on the night of October 7, 1881, when Hardee, a Black man, was found under the bed of a woman described as a "highly respectable young lady" and was suspected of intending to steal. According to a Dallas newspaper, a crowd "came very near lynching him," but he was not reported harmed.

episodes.title: Grain Valley hanging
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Grain Valley hanging was the death of an unidentified man whose body was found hanging from a tree in woods near Grain Valley Station, Jackson County, Missouri, on October 15, 1881. The man was never identified in the coverage, and newspapers offered competing explanations: that he was a detective lynched by train robbers, a suspect lynched by a vigilance committee or by farmers, or a suicide. The story drew notice because Jackson County was then the scene of prosecutions for two train robberies, and the wire report that carried it was headlined "A Detective's Fate."

episodes.title: Lynching of Ben Theophil
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Ben Theophil was the hanging of an Italian railroad laborer, also named in reports as Pete Theophil or Ben Peters, by masked men at Gunnison, Colorado, about midnight on Friday, October 28, 1881. Accused of shooting railroad contractor W. L. Hoblitzell, he was taken from a guarded room in the Gunnison court house on the night of his capture and hanged from a livery stable sign. Wire dispatches reported it nationally as a hanging 'by the citizens,' while the Elk Mountain Pilot questioned the lynching and the guarding of the prisoner.

episodes.title: Galloway robbery and lynching threat at Mount Pleasant, Pennsylvania
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Galloway robbery and lynching threat at Mount Pleasant was an episode in Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania, in October 1881, in which a crowd threatened to lynch two men arrested for robbing and beating a farmer, John Galloway, and assaulting his housekeeper. The threat, reported only by the Chicago Tribune, came to nothing: the suspects stayed under a deputy guard, one was later discharged and the other jailed at Greensburg.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jack Williams
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jack Williams took place early on October 13, 1881, when a crowd took Williams, a Black man, from the jail at Orangeburg, South Carolina, and hanged him from a tree on the edge of town. Williams had been convicted days earlier of assaulting an eleven-year-old white girl, but the jury's recommendation to mercy meant a sentence of life imprisonment instead of death. The papers stressed that the crowd overrode a completed trial, and much of the South Carolina press approved.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Boge Jackson and Henry Hill
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Boge Jackson and Henry Hill took place at Hamburg, Arkansas, on October 22, 1881, when a crowd of several thousand that had gathered to see the two Black men hanged learned that the governor had reprieved them. Many in the crowd wanted to lynch the prisoners, and one report said they were held back only with great effort, but no attack is reported. Hill's sentence was later commuted to life imprisonment, and Jackson was legally hanged at Hamburg on November 18.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of James Cunningham
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of James Cunningham took place on a road near Pillow's Bridge, outside Helena, Arkansas, in October 1881, when a disguised mob of about fifty men took three Black prisoners from officers and fired volleys at Cunningham. He was left for dead but was found alive the next morning, and the story of his survival ran in papers from Savannah to Minnesota.

episodes.title: Killing of James Truss
episodes.lead: The killing of James Truss was the fatal stabbing of a Black man at Desoto, Mississippi, on a Saturday night in late September or early October 1881. Truss died within minutes of a stab wound to the neck, and five men, four white and one Black, were said to have been involved. The killing is known from a single brief in a Memphis paper's column of Mississippi news.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jasper Delaughter
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jasper Delaughter was the hanging, in early October 1881, of a man under arrest for burglarizing a store in the southwestern Choctaw Nation, whom masked men took from a deputy marshal who was conveying him to Fort Smith. Several weeks later, officers from Fort Smith arrested a number of residents of Sevier County, Arkansas, including a physician, on charges of taking part in the lynching. None of the reports stated the race of Delaughter or of the men accused.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Redd
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Redd took place in October 1881 at Seale, Russell County, Alabama, when an armed crowd of several hundred tried to take Redd, a Black prisoner accused of murdering a Black woman, from the town jail. The sheriff and others persuaded the crowd to disperse, and although a wire dispatch passed on unconfirmed reports that Redd was later hanged, he was tried, found guilty of murder and sentenced to death in early November.

episodes.title: Lynching of Dell Lockhart, "Kid" Coulter and "Slim"
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Dell Lockhart, "Kid" Coulter and "Slim" was the killing of three jailed men by a mob at Tierra Amarilla, reported as in Colorado, in late October 1881. Lockhart and the man known as Slim were held for horse stealing and Coulter for a murder, and the lynching was attributed to the discovery of Coulter's plan to kill the guard and escape. A Denver dispatch to the Republican carried the news to papers from Maine to Arizona, where it ran mostly as a one-paragraph item.

episodes.title: Lynching of three Mexican men at Los Lunas, New Mexico
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of three Mexican men at Los Lunas took place on the night of October 7, 1881, when a mob took three men accused of murdering James Little from the jail at Las Lunas (also spelled Los Lunas), New Mexico Territory, and hanged them. The killing reached papers from California to Illinois through a brief Denver wire, and one Illinois paper headed it as a "good job" by Judge Lynch.

episodes.title: Shooting of Manning Law
episodes.lead: The shooting of Manning Law took place in late October 1881 near Buck Creek, South Carolina, when the two brothers of Mary Lewis, a white woman of Lexington County, overtook her and her new husband, a Black man, as the couple drove toward Augusta, Georgia. Law was shot in the breast in an exchange of pistol fire, and the brothers then hunted the preacher who had married the couple. Papers across the country carried the story as a case of "miscegenation," with conflicting reports on whether Law died.

episodes.title: Lynching of Lum White's wife and an elderly man near Breckville, Texas
episodes.lead: The lynching of Lum White's wife and an elderly man near Breckville, Texas, took place in October 1881, when a crowd of men took two Black prisoners from an escort bound for Carthage and shot them. The two had been held after Lum White, a Black man accused of raping and killing a white girl of about fifteen named Sloan, was shot dead at the inquest by a young man named Hart. A dispatch from Longview carried the story to papers across the country, many of which headlined the alleged crime and presented the killings as vengeance or justice.

episodes.title: Attempted mobbing of Waldo Lewis
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted mobbing of Waldo Lewis took place on the night of October 19, 1881, when four men took Lewis, a young man accused of burglary, from his house near Greenville and threatened to hang and shoot him unless he told where stolen money was hidden. Lewis escaped into a neighbor's house under gunfire and is not reported hurt, and two of the men were later jailed.

episodes.title: Sharkey County ambush of 1881
episodes.lead: The Sharkey County ambush of 1881 was the shooting of a body of Black men on their way to a Fusion political meeting in Sharkey County, Mississippi, on the night of October 28, 1881, by men hidden beside the road. Perry Thompson was killed instantly, and later accounts said two of the wounded also died. The shooters were not identified, and Mississippi papers of both parties condemned the killing as a political assassination tied to a bitter contest over county offices.

episodes.title: Wightman's barroom police shooting
episodes.lead: The Wightman's barroom police shooting was an incident on the night of 9 October 1881 in which a Savannah, Georgia, police officer named McDonald fired two shots at a group of Black men outside Wightman's barroom on South Broad street. No one was reported hurt by the shots and no arrest was made, and the Savannah Morning News reported the shooting in a single local brief.

episodes.title: Lynching of J. J. Dickison Jr.
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of J. J. Dickison Jr. was the killing of a prisoner held for an alleged murder at the Sumter county jail in Leesburg, Florida, reported in October 1881 as having occurred some two months earlier. The case drew notice because the victim's father, General Dickerson, set out to identify the lynchers and prosecute them as murderers. A grand jury indicted the jail's guards for manslaughter but failed to identify the lynchers.

episodes.title: Killing of an unnamed Black man at Taliulah, Louisiana (1881)
episodes.lead: The killing of an unnamed Black man at Taliulah, Louisiana, took place on the night of Saturday, 29 October 1881, the same day he was reported to have killed another Black man with a railway spike driver. The only known report, a one-sentence item in the Richland Beacon of Rayville, attributed his death, with a hedge, to a mob.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Thomas Olson
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Thomas Olson was a mob threat against a 17-year-old Swedish laborer held in the jail at Aurora, Illinois, on October 2, 1881, after he was accused of fatally stabbing Otto Freese the night before. Officials removed Olson secretly while a crowd gathered, and a party of about 100 young men that set out on October 4 to lynch him turned back before reaching Geneva. The Chicago Tribune covered the case beside its report of a lynching at Bloomington, and a short wire item ran across the upper Midwest.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Tom Herbert
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Tom Herbert was an attack by a mob on the jail at Kernville, Kern County, California, on the night of October 18, 1881, intended to seize and hang Herbert, a prisoner charged with murdering the mine owner who had employed him. Deputy Sheriff Ben Mitchell, who met the mob short of the jail, was shot dead, and his return fire wounded one of the attackers, Jim Cochran. The mob dispersed without reaching Herbert, and Bakersfield dispatches carried the story as far as Chicago and Memphis.

episodes.title: Lynching of William Nicholson
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of William Nicholson took place at Saunders Station, a stop on the Southern Pacific in New Mexico Territory, on the night of Thursday, October 6, 1881. He was accused of murder, specifically of "killing a man without provocation." The killing reached the national press only as a one-line addendum to reports of a double lynching at Socorro the same night.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of the Gordon brothers at Vincennes, Indiana
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of the Gordon brothers was a failed attempt by a mob at Vincennes, Indiana, to take two Black brothers named Gordon out of jail and hang them some time between October 1881 and April 1882. The brothers, accused of robbing an elderly couple, were saved by the sheriff and later convicted, after which a third brother declared that he and an uncle had committed the crime.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Russell
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Russell took place near Frankfort, Kentucky, in November 1881, after Russell, a Black man, was jailed on a charge of assaulting a white woman, Mrs. Hutchinson. Threats of lynching were made on the night of his arrest, and they reportedly grew when Mrs. Hutchinson died of her injuries. No lynching was reported; the last account had Black men guarding the jail to protect him.

episodes.title: Gold Park mining camp siege
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Gold Park mining camp siege was a mob attack in late November or early December 1881 at the Gold Park mining camp near Leadville, Colorado, in which a crowd besieged a discharged blacksmith named Bayley (also printed Bagley), accused of killing the company foreman, and blew up his cabin with giant powder. Bayley was found dead in the ruins with a bullet wound through the heart, which the original dispatch attributed to suicide, although some later news briefs said the mob had blown him up. Carried on a single Leadville dispatch, the story ran in papers across the country as an example of Western lawlessness.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bob Williams
episodes.lead: The lynching of Bob Williams was the hanging of a Black man, also reported as Robert Williams, by a crowd of about one hundred men in the woods across the Saluda River from Pelzer, South Carolina, on November 4, 1881. Williams was accused of raping a nine-year-old white girl and was taken from the guard house at Williamston. A coroner's jury found death at the hands of unknown parties, though a dispatch said the lynchers did not hide their identity and the lynching was "highly commended."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Charles Rigney
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Charles Rigney took place at Rockville, Maryland, in November 1881, after Rigney, a young Black farm hand, was accused of assaulting the five-year-old daughter of a Montrose storekeeper. The girl's father beat him and, with four other men, bound him and delivered him to the county jail, and threats to take him out and lynch him were reported for two nights. No attack came; the grand jury indicted him for an attempt rather than rape, and papers reported that the danger of lynching had passed.

episodes.title: Lynching of Chris Davis
episodes.lead: The lynching of Chris Davis took place in Athens, Ohio, in the early hours of November 21, 1881, when a mob took Davis, a Black man described as a "mulatto," from the county jail and hanged him from the bridge over the Hocking River. Davis was awaiting the grand jury on a charge of assaulting an elderly widow near Albany, and the mob extracted a confession from him by promising to return him to jail. No one was arrested, and the case drew comment as a Northern lynching, with Ohio editors divided over it and women of Albany passing resolutions in its favor.

episodes.title: Coal Valley strike and Black replacement miners (1881)
episodes.lead: The Coal Valley strike and Black replacement miners episode was a confrontation in November 1881 in Fayette County, West Virginia, in which striking coal miners at Coal Valley drove off the first group of Black miners brought from Virginia to take their places. When a second group arrived, county authorities called for troops, and two militia companies guarded the new men until the strikers dispersed. Accounts in the Wheeling Register differed on whether the strikers used threats: a visiting correspondent said they stopped "short of violence," while the county prosecutor said they threatened the men's lives.

episodes.title: Lynching of Craig and Parker Jordan
episodes.lead: The lynching of Craig and Parker Jordan was the hanging of two Black men by a mob in Leflore County, Mississippi, on the night of November 26, 1881, after they were accused of assassinating Robert Catlin, a white man. Both were said to have confessed after their capture and were hanged to a tree near a place the dispatches called Shepherdstown. Wire stories carried the case across the country, and Mississippi papers greeted it as "speedy vengeance."

episodes.title: Lynching of Ed Maxwell
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Ed Maxwell took place on November 19, 1881, at Durand, Pepin County, Wisconsin, when a crowd overpowered the officers guarding Edward Maxwell, alias Ed Williams, and hanged him from a tree in the court-house yard. Maxwell had just pleaded not guilty to the murder of the Coleman brothers and been committed for trial. The case drew national notice for a coroner's verdict that he had died by falling down the court-house steps, and for a feud among Minnesota and Wisconsin papers over what had happened.

episodes.title: Marion election riot
episodes.lead: The Marion election riot was a shooting at the polls at Marion Station, Lauderdale County, Mississippi, on election day, November 8, 1881, followed that afternoon by a sheriff's posse's siege of the house of Ed Vance, a white Republican, where Black men had taken refuge. Four white men died of the shooting at the polls; at the house the posse killed Vance's son John, lost one of its own men and fired on fleeing Black men, with reports of Black dead ranging from none to fifteen. Wire reports blamed armed Black men, while Republican papers printed accounts in which white Democrats began the attack.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of J. M. Garrison
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of J. M. Garrison took place at Winfield, Du Page County, Illinois, in late November 1881, when farmers who supplied his cheese factory gathered with a rope to hang him after the factory burned. Garrison's creditors accused him of setting the fire to avoid paying them, but the county sheriff intervened and took him to jail at Wheaton. Chicago dispatches about his escape were reprinted under headings such as "Escaped Lynching" in papers from Delaware to Minnesota and Wisconsin.

episodes.title: Lynching of James P. Holland
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of James P. Holland was the hanging of a prisoner accused of murder by masked men who broke into the jail at Dardanelle, Yell County, Arkansas, about midnight on November 26–27, 1881. Holland had escaped jail before a verdict in his trial for an 1879 killing and had been returned from Tennessee hours earlier; he was hanged in the jail yard where a mob had hanged a man named Taylor months before. Papers nationwide carried it as another Arkansas lynching, while a Russellville paper printed a letter defending it.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Joe Smith
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Joe Smith took place at Weedsport, New York, on November 18, 1881, when a mob tried to take Smith, a prisoner accused of outraging and nearly murdering a young woman, from the constable who had brought him there. The constable held the mob off, and the sheriff and a posse kept guard over the prisoner, who "narrowly escaped lynching by the villagers." The episode ran as a short wire item in papers from Maine to Georgia and Tennessee; none of them stated Smith's race.

episodes.title: Whipping of Jordan Denny
episodes.lead: The whipping of Jordan Denny was a night attack on an elderly Black mail carrier at his home in Lancaster, Garrard County, Kentucky, in early November 1881, shortly before his planned wedding. Accounts disagree on the night, the attackers and his injuries, and papers in Kentucky, Texas and Utah all treated it as a comic item.

episodes.title: Caperton Station shooting
episodes.lead: The Caperton Station shooting was the shooting of a Black striking miner named Lewis by J. W. St. Clair, the prosecuting attorney of Fayette County, West Virginia, at Caperton Station on the evening of November 1, 1881. St. Clair fired on Lewis as he tried to escape after his arrest, and the first dispatches reported him killed. Later reports said he had only been wounded, and one Washington paper questioned whether he had been shot for striking or for being Black.

episodes.title: Masked-band attacks on Black residents of Kenton, Tennessee
episodes.lead: The masked-band attacks on Black residents of Kenton, Tennessee, were a series of raids in the autumn of 1881 in which masked men repeatedly entered the Obion County town and whipped and maltreated Black men, women and children. Residents appealed to the governor, and Governor Hawkins offered a $250 reward for the arrest and conviction of those responsible. Tennessee papers carried the raids as brief state-news items, and at least one Northern paper presented them as a remnant of the Ku Klux.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Charles Madder
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Charles Madder was an attack by a mob of several hundred people on the jail at Tiffin, Ohio, early on November 7, 1881, in an effort to seize Madder, a Heidelberg College divinity student held on the charge of shooting Phoebe Bernard. The sheriff's armed posse drove the crowd off after a fight in which officers were injured, and Madder was moved secretly to Fremont and then to the Toledo jail. The repulse was carried by wire across the country, while a Tiffin dispatch in the paper of Madder's home county called the reports false.

episodes.title: Lynching of Massey Hill
episodes.lead: The lynching of Massey Hill took place on the night of Saturday, November 5, 1881, when a mob took Hill, a Black man, from the jail at Manchester, Tennessee, and killed him. Hill had been accused of attempting to rape a little girl near the town, and two papers reported that he was hanged. A one-sentence Nashville dispatch carried the news across the country, where it was often printed beside the lynching of Robert Williams in South Carolina the same week.

episodes.title: Mendota mob threat against a burglar (1881)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Mendota mob threat against a burglar was an incident at Mendota, Illinois, reported in October 1881, in which a mob put a noose around the neck of a man accused of burglary and made him choose between hanging and promising to plead guilty. The man promised, and the mob dispersed without killing him. The story survives only as a short unattributed paragraph that newspapers ran with an ironic comment on the mob's idea of justice.

episodes.title: Killing of Robert Harvey
episodes.lead: The killing of Robert Harvey was the killing of a Black man by Sheriff Lewis of Austin County, Texas, reported in a telegram from Brenham dated November 28, 1881. The telegram said Harvey was killed while resisting arrest and described him as "a cow thief and a bad negro." The two-sentence report ran in Waco and Dallas papers and is the only account found.

episodes.title: Rockdale County posse killing (1881)
episodes.lead: The Rockdale County posse killing was the fatal shooting of an unnamed Black man by a posse in Rockdale County, Georgia, reported from Atlanta on November 23, 1881. The man, accused of robbing a store, was shot dead after he refused an order to stop, and a jury returned a verdict of justifiable homicide. The brief dispatch ran in papers from Georgia to Texas and Pennsylvania, which headed it variously as a robber's death or as "justifiable homicide."

episodes.title: Lynching of Sandy King and Russian Bill
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Sandy King and Russian Bill was the hanging of two men accused of stealing stock by over a dozen masked men at the jail in Shakespeare, New Mexico, at about 2 a.m. on November 9, 1881. The two, described as members of a "noted cowboy gang" held for trial, were hanged from a joist after the mob seized their guard. A Tucson dispatch carried the story to papers across the country within a day, while correspondents in New Mexico and Arizona wrote of the hanging with approval or mockery.

episodes.title: Killing of Felix Burke
episodes.lead: The killing of Felix Burke was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Deputy Sheriff McDonald in Monroe County, Arkansas, in early November 1881, while the deputy was trying to arrest him on a charge of stealing a mule. McDonald was badly wounded in the exchange of fire, and the episode reached distant newspapers only as a brief telegraphic crime item.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Robinson
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Robinson took place in Kanawha County, West Virginia, in November 1881, after Robinson was accused of shooting and killing Allen Belcher, the town marshal of Malden, on November 15. Telegraphic reports said a mob was coming or organizing to take Robinson from the Charleston jail and hang him, and guards, militia and federal marshals were posted around the jail. No attack on the jail was reported, and a Charleston correspondent wrote that no lynching had ever been planned.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at Adrian, Illinois
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching at Adrian, Illinois, took place on November 9, 1881, when a mob at Adrian, in Hancock County, tried to seize a young Black farm hand from the officers bringing him back from Peoria and shot him three times. He had been accused of assaulting a farmer's wife, Mrs. Kenkel (also spelled Kunkel), and officers carried him under guard to the county jail at Carthage, where he was reported to be dying. Short wire accounts of the shooting ran in papers from Wisconsin to Mississippi and New Mexico over the next ten days.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Alonzo Garner
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Alonzo Garner took place in St. Paul, Minnesota, on Sunday night, December 18, 1881, when a crowd nearly lynched Garner after he was arrested on a charge of setting several fires near the Post Siding. Garner survived, was indicted for arson, and was convicted the next month of attempting to burn a store. The only report of the attempt on him was a single clause in the St. Paul Daily Globe's police-court column, and no paper gave his race.

episodes.title: Hanging of three Mexican men on the Bandera road
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The hanging of three Mexican men on the Bandera road was the killing of three unnamed men whose bodies were found hanging from a tree northwest of San Antonio, Texas, on or shortly before 17 December 1881. The men were supposed to be robbers of travelers, and the papers said they had probably been lynched by German farmers of the neighborhood. Distant papers reported it only through a brief telegraphic item, and no one was identified.

episodes.title: Lynching of "Arizona Bill" at Pittman Valley
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of "Arizona Bill" took place at Pittman Valley, Arizona Territory, around Christmas Day 1881, when an armed party took the man, named by Prescott papers as William Lewis, from a deputy sheriff's guard and hanged and shot him. He was accused of shooting Charles Collins, known as "Shorty", during a quarrel, and the story travelled from Prescott papers to Tombstone, Los Angeles, Iowa and West Virginia.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Bright Picket
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Bright Picket was an attack by a mob of one hundred masked men on a jail in Texas, reported in early December 1881, with the object of lynching Picket, a prisoner held there. The sheriff, Hopkins, assisted by his wife, fought the mob off, and no one is reported killed. The episode is known from a single brief that credited the sheriff and his wife with the defense.

episodes.title: Killing of Charles Flowers
episodes.lead: The killing of Charles Flowers was the fatal shooting of a Black chain-gang convict by officers pursuing him after an escape near Savannah, Georgia, in December 1881. Flowers was wounded and recaptured at a camp about ten miles from the city and died at the Georgia Infirmary on the night of Wednesday, January 4, 1882. A coroner's jury found that he died of a gunshot wound from a gun held by one of his pursuers, John alias Samuel Golden, and called the killing manslaughter.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Charles Tippit
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Charles Tippit was a half-hanging of a man accused of petty theft at Star Hill, near Cherry Creek, Nevada, in late December 1881. Three men were charged, but a justice court dismissed the felony charge as more joke than earnest, and a jury on a lesser assault charge failed to agree. The local weekly, the White Pine News, treated the affair as a Christmas "lark" and followed it through two hearings.

episodes.title: Lynching of Dave Bumpers
episodes.lead: The lynching of Dave Bumpers was the hanging of a Black eighteen-year-old by a mob at Athens, Georgia, in mid-December 1881. Bumpers had been accused of assaulting Mrs. Driscoll in her home, and the mob took him from the officers holding him and hanged him to an oak tree with a plow line. Northern and Southern papers carried the news as a short wire item, several under headlines that called him a "brute" or a "miscreant."

episodes.title: Shooting of Dave Martin
episodes.lead: The shooting of Dave Martin was the wounding of a Black man by a policeman at Peak's Station, near Alston, South Carolina, during the Christmas holidays of 1881. Martin was first reported killed while "resisting a policeman," but a later notice in the same Winnsboro paper said he was alive and expected to recover.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of David McMillan
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of David McMillan took place at the jail in Greenfield, Massachusetts, on the evening of December 6, 1881, when a crowd tried to seize McMillan, who was accused of shooting the parish priest, Father McCarthy. Officers holding the prisoner displayed revolvers, the crowd fell back, and McMillan was lodged in jail unharmed. Wire reports of the scene, under headings such as "Fear of Lynching" and "Safe in Jail", ran in papers across the country.

episodes.title: Lynching of a cowboy at Deming
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of a cowboy at Deming is known from a single anecdote, headlined "Wild Shooting in Arizona," printed in The Home Journal of Winchester, Tennessee, on December 7, 1881. According to the anecdote, an unnamed cowboy accidentally shot and killed a young newcomer in the street and "was lynched soon after." The account gives no date, names, or race for anyone involved, and its writer was unsure even of the town.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Ed Grayham
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Ed Grayham took place at Brookhaven, Mississippi, on a Saturday at the end of December 1881, when a large number of men came to the town jail to lynch Ed. Grayham, a young Black prisoner accused of raping a girl of about five. The jailer had sent the prisoner away in advance, and the men left after searching the empty jail. Grayham, spelled Graham in later reports, was convicted of rape in February 1882 and sentenced to life in the penitentiary.

episodes.title: Killing of Ed Nelms
episodes.lead: The killing of Ed Nelms was the fatal shooting of Ed Nelms, a Black man who had escaped from a Mississippi jail while under sentence of death, by Memphis Chief of Police W. C. Davis on the Arkansas bank of the Mississippi River opposite Memphis early on December 29, 1881. A coroner's jury at Memphis found the same day that Davis was "thoroughly justifiable." The Memphis dailies praised the chief at length, and a brief dispatch carried the story nationwide.

episodes.title: Fairfax County vigilance committee expulsion (1881)
episodes.lead: The Fairfax County vigilance committee expulsion was the forced departure of an unnamed Black man from part of Fairfax County, Virginia, in early December 1881, after a newly formed vigilance committee ordered him to leave for living with a white woman. He left almost at once, and the one newspaper report of it treated the episode as a joke.

episodes.title: Lynching of Francis Jordan
episodes.lead: The lynching of Francis Jordan was the reported killing of a Black woman at Las Vegas, New Mexico Territory, in late 1881, for the alleged murder of a Mrs. Feste. The only known account is a one-sentence item in a Kentucky weekly, which gave no date, no description of who killed her and no circumstances.

episodes.title: Shooting of Hampton Price
episodes.lead: The shooting of Hampton Price was the fatal shooting of a Black man described as a "negro conjurer and so called doctor" by Oliver, the town sergeant of Franklin, Southampton County, Virginia, in December 1881. According to the reports, Price struck the officer with a black-jack when the sergeant pressed him to return fifty cents paid for a charm, and Oliver shot him in the back as he fled. Oliver was charged with the shooting, and Virginia papers took note when both witnesses for the Commonwealth died within days, leaving the prosecution without evidence.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of George Berry
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of George Berry took place at Texarkana, Arkansas, on December 30, 1881, when railroad men took Berry from officers who were bringing him to jail and tried to hang him for the shooting of John Smith. The hanging failed because the cotton scales they used were too low, and the men handed Berry back to the officers while vowing to hang him if Smith died. The story ran by telegraph in papers from Richmond to Los Angeles, most of which predicted a lynching that night.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of George Mills
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of George Mills took place at Hannibal, Missouri, in December 1881, when a posse of fifteen men who seized Mills on an accusation of attempted rape barely kept him from being lynched. Mills was handed over to the authorities, and the story ran as a short wire item in several out-of-state papers on December 21.

episodes.title: Lynching of George Pfeiffer
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of George Pfeiffer was the reported hanging in Kansas, around the turn of 1882, of a Pennsylvania-raised man charged with robbing the mails. According to a dispatch from Lock Haven, Pennsylvania, he had confessed to mail robbery, arson and poisoning his wife, and Kansans, judging a trial useless, hanged him "by lynch law."

episodes.title: Anniston calaboose shooting
episodes.lead: The Anniston calaboose shooting was the killing of two Black men, named in the press only as Greenwood and Hammond, by the town marshal and his deputy at the lock-up in Anniston, Alabama, in late November or early December 1881. The officers fired when a crowd of Black men pressed them as they jailed a prisoner, and an inquest and a preliminary hearing cleared them. Newspapers across the country carried the story as a riot in 'a mining town' put down by police.

episodes.title: Hickory church burning
episodes.lead: The Hickory church burning was an attack in which a Black church at Hickory, Mississippi, was fired into and burned on a Monday night in late December 1881, and the town's calaboose was burned the same night. Three white men and a Black man were arrested on the charges, and a judge went to Hickory to investigate amid local alarm at the failure of officials to check lawlessness.

episodes.title: Beating of a hotel porter in Hinton, West Virginia (1881)
episodes.lead: The beating of a hotel porter in Hinton, West Virginia, was an assault on a Black porter by a man named Farris on the morning of 25 December 1881. Farris was arrested and brought before the mayor, but his friends' anger at the arresting officer led to an armed attack on the town's police the next night. Only the Richmond Dispatch's Hinton correspondent reported the beating; other papers carried only the attack on the police.

episodes.title: Mob hanging of Ilen Pettis
episodes.lead: The mob hanging of Ilen Pettis took place in White County, Arkansas, in late December 1881, when ten masked men took Pettis, a Black prisoner accused of robbery, from jail and hanged him from a tree limb until he confessed. The men returned him alive to the jailer and handed the recovered money to the sheriff. It is known only from one Chicago Tribune dispatch, which reported it approvingly.

episodes.title: Killing of Isaac Hicks
episodes.lead: The killing of Isaac Hicks was the fatal shooting of a Black man by two Savannah policemen at a railway section camp outside Savannah, Georgia, in late December 1881, while they were searching for a different man. Hicks ran from a shanty when the officers came to the door, was shot in three places, and died the next morning at the police barracks. The Savannah Morning News headlined the case "The Wrong Man Killed," and under a coroner's jury's majority verdict the officers were held for the grand jury.

episodes.title: Round Oak dance killings
episodes.lead: The Round Oak dance killings took place on the night of Monday, December 26, 1881, at a Black dance near Round Oak in Jones County, Georgia, where a young white farmer named Gray was fatally stabbed in a fight and shot dead three Black brothers named Jackson before dying himself. A brief Macon dispatch carried the story to papers from Maine to Texas, which headlined the four deaths at a "negro dance."

episodes.title: Sibley's Mill shootings
episodes.lead: The Sibley's Mill shootings were a pair of fatal shootings in Baldwin County, Alabama, opposite Mobile, in late December 1881, in which a deputy sheriff and an unnamed Black man accused of ambushing the deputy's brother shot each other during an arrest. Deputy Sheriff Abe Johnson died within fifteen minutes, and a crowd that set out after the wounded suspect found him dead near a swamp. A Mobile dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, several of which presented the suspect's death as swift vengeance.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Brodie and Shadrack Hester
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Brodie and Shadrack Hester took place in the early hours of December 1, 1881, at Oxford, Granville County, North Carolina, when a party of masked men took the two Black prisoners from the county jail and hanged them. Both men were held on a charge of murdering Thomas M. Lynch, an Oxford jeweler, and had not been tried. The Raleigh wire carried the story nationally the same day, and several North Carolina papers presented the hanging as just retribution.

episodes.title: Killing of John Rhodes
episodes.lead: The killing of John Rhodes was the shooting of a Black man in his cabin on the Carson place, near Friars Point, Mississippi, by two masked men on a Saturday night in late 1881, probably December 3. Rhodes died of a shot to the head, and the only report supposed that the men had meant not to kill him but to frighten him off the place.

episodes.title: Mob attack on the King family (Montgomery County, Missouri)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The mob attack on the King family was a night raid on December 30, 1881, in which an armed mob fired into the King family's cabin near Americus, in Montgomery County, Missouri, killing Mrs. Nancy Austin and wounding Mrs. King and at least one son. It came the night after one of the King brothers was shot dead while trying to force his way into a neighbor's house. The story ran nationally in January 1882 and again in March, when the family filed damage suits against members of the mob.

episodes.title: Lynching of L. M. Bell
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of L. M. Bell was the hanging of a planter, called Colonel Bell, by a mob near Hamburg, Arkansas, close to the Louisiana line, on the night of December 27, 1881. Bell was accused of beating his wife so badly that she died at Christmas, and neighbors took him from his home and hanged him to a tree. Wire reports carried the story across the country, and several papers presented the lynching as deserved.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Loula Tyler
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Loula Tyler took place near White's Station, east of Memphis, on 22 December 1881, when a Black girl of about seventeen accused of choking a schoolgirl was 'with difficulty' saved from lynching. She was jailed in Memphis to await the grand jury; the episode is known from a single Memphis Public Ledger report.

episodes.title: Disappearance and reported lynching of Mark Thompson
episodes.lead: The disappearance and reported lynching of Mark Thompson took place near Dawson, Georgia, in late November or early December 1881, when white men seized Thompson, a young Black man, as a suspect in an attack on a man named John E. Moreland and carried him away. He was reported beaten to death, but searchers found only a bloody shirt and socks buried in a swamp. A wire dispatch carried the story to papers from Pennsylvania to California, most of which headlined the robbery rather than the killing.

episodes.title: Killing of Henry Mitchell
episodes.lead: The killing of Henry Mitchell was the fatal shooting of a Black workman during a row between white and Black workmen at the Ohio Valley cement mill, six miles from Jeffersonville, Indiana, on the night of December 24, 1881. Mitchell was shot by a local man named Long, who escaped. Newspapers from West Virginia to Minnesota and Mississippi carried a brief wire dispatch about it among the many Christmas crimes of that year.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Morgan Richards
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Morgan Richards took place near Gore, Hocking County, Ohio, on December 29, 1881, when a mob tried to take Richards, a farm hand accused of murdering his aunt, from the officers who had arrested him. The officers repulsed the mob and lodged him in the jail at Logan. Wire reports carried the story nationally as a crime item, and several predicted that he would still be lynched.

episodes.title: Burning of the Scott home and expulsion of the Scott family from Salina, Kansas
episodes.lead: The burning of the Scott home and expulsion of the Scott family from Salina, Kansas, took place on the night of December 27, 1881, when a mob set fire to the house of Mrs. Scott, a Black woman, and ordered her to leave town with her daughters. The family went to Denver, where the Denver Star took up the case as an outrage left unpunished because of their color.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Neal
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Neal took place in Wilmington, Delaware, on the afternoon of 6 December 1881, when a jury acquitted Neal, a Black man, of an alleged rape of a white woman, Mrs. Gosser. Because of threats to lynch him, he was hurried from the courtroom to a waiting carriage and driven out of the state into Pennsylvania. The case drew attention because the verdict was condemned across the state, and several papers warned that it would bring on lynch law in Delaware.

episodes.title: Lynching of Nicholas Puct
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Nicholas Puct was the hanging of a man by unnamed lynchers on a grapevine in Texas in December 1881. It is known from a single line in a wire roundup of seven killings in the Texas border country, which gave no place, accusation or race for the victim.

episodes.title: Half-hanging of a thief at Niptown
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The half-hanging of a thief at Niptown was a non-fatal vigilante hanging of an unnamed man accused of petty theft, carried out by a self-described 'half-way lynching party' on or about Tuesday, 27 December 1881. The man survived, and the local paper that reported it warned that a further offense would bring a real lynching.

episodes.title: Assault on an elderly Black man on the Cairo levee (1881)
episodes.lead: The assault on an elderly Black man on the Cairo levee was a beating of an unnamed "old negro man" by a gang on the Ohio levee at Cairo, Illinois, on Christmas Day 1881. One of the attackers, a white man named Wm. Carroll, was arrested about two weeks later and fined five dollars and costs.

episodes.title: Killing of Patton and Mallory at Independence, Colorado
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The killing of Patton and Mallory took place at Independence, a mining camp about twenty miles west of Leadville, Colorado, shortly after dark on or about December 16, 1881, when townspeople chased down and shot two men described as desperadoes. The pair had been firing revolvers in the streets, and a crowd 'riddled' them with bullets, after which a vigilance committee formed to hang others of their kind, who fled. A single Leadville dispatch carried the story across the country, where papers headlined it as summary justice.

episodes.title: Pratt coal mines arrest shooting
episodes.lead: The Pratt coal mines arrest shooting was the killing of an unnamed Black man by an officer at the Pratt coal mines in Jefferson County, Alabama, reported in a Montgomery dispatch of December 9, 1881. According to the dispatch, the man resisted arrest and took up a shotgun, and the officer shot him before he could fire. The item ran as a brief telegraphic crime notice in papers from Pennsylvania to Texas.

episodes.title: Death of an unidentified Black man near Reagan, Texas (1881)
episodes.lead: The death of an unidentified Black man near Reagan, Texas, came to light around Christmas 1881, when his body was found on a railroad track near the town after two trains had reportedly passed over it. The Waco Daily Examiner, the only paper found to report it, suggested that unknown persons had killed and robbed him and left his body on the track to hide the crime.

episodes.title: Lynching of Richard Jennings
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Richard Jennings took place at Austin, Nevada, early on December 14, 1881, when a party of masked men took him from the county jail and hanged him from the front of the Court-house. Jennings, a miner newly arrived from Grass Valley, California, had been jailed on a charge of shooting John A. Barrett, a well-liked Austin resident, on December 12. The story ran by wire across the country, and Nevada papers largely endorsed the hanging as a warning to armed roughs.

episodes.title: Police shooting of Sam Duckett
episodes.lead: The police shooting of Sam Duckett took place on Christmas afternoon, 25 December 1881, in South Washington, D.C., when Officer Branson shot Duckett, a Black man, in the head during a street fight over the arrest of his sister, Ellen Duckett. Duckett survived, was arrested three days later, pleaded guilty in Police Court and was fined $10 or thirty days. Washington's daily papers told the story as an attack on two policemen by a Black crowd.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at Searcy, Arkansas (1881)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching at Searcy was an effort by a party of men in Searcy, Arkansas, in December 1881 to hang an unnamed Black man at the urging of a visitor who offered to show the town's young men how to "hang a nigger." Before the hanging could be carried out, the lynchers were attacked by a large number of persons, and the instigator fled. The only known account is a mocking item in the Searcy Record, reprinted in the Memphis Daily Appeal.

episodes.title: Driving out of Black strikebreakers at Coal Valley, West Virginia
episodes.lead: The driving out of Black strikebreakers at Coal Valley, West Virginia, took place in late 1881, when striking coal miners in Fayette County turned back the first group of Black miners that operators had brought from Virginia to replace them. Troops were then called to guard a second group, and the Wheeling Register printed two conflicting accounts of how serious the confrontation had been.

episodes.title: Shooting of Thomas Thompson
episodes.lead: The shooting of Thomas Thompson was the shooting of a Black man, described as "colored," by an officer named Griffith at Newark, Ohio, reported in December 1881. The only report found gave the officer's circumstance, that Thompson was "attempting to escape," and said nothing of whether he survived.

episodes.title: Whipping of a Black barber in Washington, Georgia
episodes.lead: The whipping of a Black barber in Washington, Georgia, was an assault in which unnamed men took out a "negro barber" of the town, who had said he knew where Confederate gold was buried, and whipped him "nearly to death" to make him tell where it was. The Atlanta Constitution mentioned it in December 1881, in an article defending Jefferson Davis against a charge that he had misused Confederate funds.

episodes.title: Lynching of William Allen
episodes.lead: The lynching of William Allen was the hanging of a Black prisoner by a party of masked men near Warwick Court House, Virginia, on the night of December 5, 1881. Allen had been jailed three days earlier, accused of fatally stabbing a white man, William S. Selater, near Newport News. The lynchers reportedly obtained him with a forged transfer order, and the one man arrested, a white barber named Thomas Valentine, was discharged for lack of evidence.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching at Lafayette, Alabama (1881)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching at Lafayette, Alabama, took place in December 1881, when a crowd was reported going to the Lafayette jail to demand a Black prisoner accused of killing a merchant in Chambers County. A Montgomery dispatch said there was a "strong probability" that the man had been hanged, and papers from Savannah to Sacramento repeated the story, one of them as an accomplished lynching. No later report confirming or denying his death appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Lynching ruse against William Miller
episodes.lead: The lynching ruse against William Miller took place at the jail in Aberdeen, Mississippi, on the night of December 24, 1881, when Miller, a Black prisoner held as accomplice in a triple murder, was taken from his cell "under the threat and pretext of being lynched." The removal left his cellmate, the white suspect W. Robert Jones, alone to be questioned, and Jones confessed. Both men were convicted at a special term of court in January 1882 and sentenced to hang.

episodes.title: Niptown half-way lynching
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Niptown half-way lynching was the nonfatal hanging of an accused petty thief by a group that a Nevada newspaper item called "the boys up at Niptown," on a Tuesday in late December 1881, probably December 27. The man was hung up until he was bruised and let live, and the item warned that a further offense would bring his death at the hands of "Judge Lynch." A brief item about it, credited to the Cherry Creek News, circulated in several Nevada papers in the following weeks.

episodes.title: Vigilante hangings near Reynosa, Mexico (1881)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The vigilante hangings near Reynosa were the killings in December 1881 of three men described as 'noted bandits' and of a fourth man, Zefarino Mercado, by Mexican vigilants who called themselves a 'Commission', in Mexico near and south of Reynosa. The news reached American papers through dispatches from Brownsville, Texas, and some later briefs placed the hangings in Brownsville itself.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Lincoln County arson suspects (1882)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Lincoln County arson suspects took place in January 1882 in Lincoln County, Georgia, where Black men jailed on an accusation of trying to burn the house of P. A. Cox near Lincolnton were threatened with lynching. County officials kept the prisoners from the threatened lynching, though an Augusta dispatch said fear for their lives persisted.

episodes.title: False report of the lynching of Calvin Luckey
episodes.lead: The false report of the lynching of Calvin Luckey was a January 1882 newspaper story that a mob in Randolph County, West Virginia, had hanged a Black man named Luckey after he shot the white father of the woman he had married. First printed by the Wheeling Register and copied by papers from Virginia to Dakota, the story was called a lie by the Randolph County press within a week. Papers that had carried it then retracted it as 'wholly untrue' or contradicted it.

episodes.title: Rumored lynching of Charles LaFour
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The rumored lynching of Charles LaFour was an unconfirmed report, printed in Wisconsin in early January 1882, that a man known to the Fond du Lac police had killed a man at Superior City on Lake Superior and been lynched by a mob. The story rested on a rumor that the Fond du Lac Commonwealth said it could not verify, and no confirming report appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Hickory church burning
episodes.lead: The Hickory church burning was a night attack at Hickory, Mississippi, in which a Black church was fired into and burned and the town calaboose was burned, around the turn of 1881–82. Three white men and a Black man were arrested on the charges, and a judge went to the town to investigate.
