episodes.title: Lynching of James McHan
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of James McHan took place at Pecos, New Mexico Territory, about thirty miles south of Las Vegas, on the night of June 8, 1882, when a mob hanged a young railroad section hand accused of shooting a co-worker. McHan had fled after the killing of John Graves, was captured by about forty men and put under guard, and was then taken from his guards and hanged to a bridge in the station yard. A brief wire report of the case ran in papers from Washington to Nevada in the following two weeks.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jim Mitchell
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jim Mitchell took place on the night of June 14, 1882, at Mount Sterling, Kentucky, where armed men took Mitchell, a Black man, from the jail and hanged him from a railroad trestle. Mitchell had been jailed that day, accused of assaulting the wife of a local farmer. The Louisville dispatch that carried the story across the country said the whole community approved of the lynching.

episodes.title: Sale of John Hanson
episodes.lead: The sale of John Hanson was the public auction of a Black man into a year's servitude at the courthouse door in Louisville, Kentucky, on June 14, 1882, as punishment for vagrancy. A city scavenger bought him for two dollars. Papers across the country reported it as a return of slavery, the first such sale in the city since before the Civil War.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Johnson
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Johnson was the hanging of a 17-year-old Black youth by a crowd at Rock Hill, South Carolina, early on the morning of June 12, 1882. Johnson had been accused of assaulting Alice McDowell, a white girl, the day before, and was taken from a guard and hanged from a tree on Main Street. A coroner's jury found that he was hanged by persons unknown, and a Charleston wire carried the news to papers across the country.

episodes.title: Brighton train attack on Joliet strikebreakers
episodes.lead: The Brighton train attack was an assault by about fifty striking iron workers on non-union laborers of the Joliet Iron and Steel Company aboard a Chicago & Alton train at Brighton, Chicago, on the evening of June 1, 1882. Most of those dragged out and beaten were Black workers, and a stray shot wounded Judge N. J. Pillsbury of the Illinois appellate court, a passenger. No one was reported killed, several men were arrested, and the story ran nationally within coverage of the iron strike.

episodes.title: Lynching of Milan Howard
episodes.lead: The lynching of Milan Howard took place at the bridge over Bonfouca, in St. Tammany Parish, Louisiana, in June 1882, when about sixty men took Howard, a Black man accused of rape, from a constable and hanged him from the bridge. The parish paper approved the killing, and the parish later paid for his burial as a man "hung by unknown parties." Outside Louisiana the hanging circulated mainly as a joke item claiming that Oscar Wilde had watched it from a train.

episodes.title: Lynching of Morgan Hamilton
episodes.lead: The lynching of Morgan Hamilton was the shooting of a Black farm worker by a party of men carrying an arrest warrant in a field near Booneville, Mississippi, on the morning of Saturday, June 17, 1882. Hamilton had been accused of the murder of Miss Serena Benton and released by the inquest jury; the eight or ten men who went to re-arrest him shot him as he ran, and the sheriff set out after them. A Mississippi correspondent called the killing an outrage committed "on mere suspicion," while wire copy carried it across the country as the shooting of an accused murderer.

episodes.title: Lynching of Nathan Laird
episodes.lead: The lynching of Nathan Laird was the hanging of a Black prisoner by a masked mob that took him from the jail at Sardis, Mississippi, early on the morning of June 21, 1882. Laird, named 'Nathan Lucid' in the wire report and 'Frank Layard' in a Memphis paper, was awaiting trial on a charge of raping or assaulting members of a white widow's household. The Sardis paper gave a detailed account of the jail raid, while papers across the country carried a one-sentence wire item.

episodes.title: Lynching of Navajo Frank
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Navajo Frank was the hanging of Francisco Tajoya, an Indian prisoner known as Navajo Frank, by a crowd of citizens at Las Vegas, New Mexico, in late June 1882. Accused of lassoing a man named R. H. Hutter and dragging him through the street, he was captured by a posse, then taken from the jail by force and hanged from a telegraph pole. A St. Louis telegraphic special carried the story nationally, often under headlines that cast the hanging as a fitting punishment.

episodes.title: Lewisville cabin shooting and rapes (1882)
episodes.lead: The Lewisville cabin shooting and rapes took place on the night of June 4, 1882, near Lewisville, Texas, when a group of armed men shot into the cabin of Perry Bolin, a Black man, forced their way in and raped two Black women. The accusation surfaced at a hearing on a separate complaint by two farmers whom the same men had shot at that night, and officers were reported to be pursuing the three accused.

episodes.title: Stabbing of Bernard McNally during the Baltimore G.A.R. parade
episodes.lead: The McNally stabbing in Baltimore took place on the evening of 21 June 1882, when boys threw stones at a parading Black division of the Grand Army of the Republic and a member of the column fatally stabbed Bernard McNally, a youth standing at the corner of Madison and Constitution streets. George H. Brightman, the Black vice-commander of Lincoln Post, was charged with murder after a coroner's jury named him, but he was acquitted in December 1882 when the state conceded its evidence was insufficient.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Herman Schmidt
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Herman Schmidt followed the shooting of a saloon keeper's wife in Chico, California, on the night of June 24, 1882. Wire dispatches said a crowd had gathered and that he would probably be lynched before morning, but he was instead tried at Oroville, convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to hang. Later reports drew notice to how quickly the court had disposed of the case.

episodes.title: Third Ward polling-place assaults, Wilmington, 1882
episodes.lead: The Third Ward polling-place assaults took place on 3 June 1882 at the Third Ward polls in Wilmington, Delaware, during a municipal election, when a crowd of Democrats drove colored voters from the polls and beat two men who vouched for them. Mr. Burchall was badly beaten and Edmund Mitchell nearly killed, according to the Republican Daily Republican, the only paper found to report the assaults.

episodes.title: Lynching of Thomas Wall and Trinidad Charlie
episodes.lead: The lynching of Thomas Wall and Trinidad Charlie took place at Rico, Colorado, at about 2 a.m. on June 16, 1882, when a party entered the town jail, took out the two prisoners and hanged them in a small cabin opposite. The men were accused of killing Rico's marshal, and the wire report of their deaths ran in papers across the country under headings such as "Two Murderers Lynched in Colorado." Only one syndicated brief described them as "two colored desperadoes."

episodes.title: Burning of Thomas J. Archer's farm, Cardington, Ohio
episodes.lead: The burning of Thomas J. Archer's farm took place near Cardington, Ohio, on the night of June 5, 1882, when a mob burned the house, barn and farm buildings of Archer, a Black man, while he was held in jail for shooting three people. The sheriff kept Archer from a crowd that had threatened to lynch him, and the story circulated in Ohio and beyond because the quarrel was said to have begun with neighbors refusing to call him "Mister Archer."

episodes.title: Lynching of three men at Butlerville, Arkansas
episodes.lead: The lynching of three men at Butlerville, Arkansas, took place on the night of Sunday, June 4, 1882, when a mob took three Black men from officers at Butlerville, in Lonoke County, and hanged them to a tree. The men, who were not named, were accused of assaulting a thirteen-year-old girl, Annie Bridges, although an earlier report had called the story untrue. A Little Rock dispatch of June 5 carried the news to papers across the country, many under headlines presenting the hanging as just punishment.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Tibbetts
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Tibbetts took place at Perham, Otter Tail County, Minnesota, at about one o'clock on the morning of June 9, 1882, when twenty men broke into the jail and hanged him from a ladder set against a telegraph pole. Tibbetts, a youth whose age the papers gave as anywhere from 12 to 17, was accused of murdering two men near the Red Eye about ten days earlier. Papers across the country carried it as the story of a "boy murderer" corrupted by dime novels, and several editorials used it to condemn lynching.

episodes.title: Killing of William Broder
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The killing of William Broder was the shooting of a saloon keeper by vigilantes at Park Station, Montana Territory, on the night of June 15, 1882. Broder was called to the door of his saloon and shot dead, the vigilantes' stated reason being that his place was a resort for thieves. The news reached the wider press only as a one-sentence wire item, which Pacific coast dailies and Midwestern weeklies reprinted over the following two weeks.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Tolly
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Tolly was the hanging of a young Black man by a mob at Elizabethtown, Illinois, on the evening of Monday, June 26, 1882. He was accused of trying to break into the house of Mrs. Howe, but she could not identify him, and a witness said he had been elsewhere. Papers across the country carried the story because the man hanged was believed to be innocent, under headlines such as "Hanged the Wrong Man."

episodes.title: Charlieville shooting (1881)
episodes.lead: The Charlieville shooting was the shooting of an unnamed Black man at Charlieville, Louisiana, on a Monday in late August 1881. He was reported to be mortally wounded, and the men who shot him were said to be still at large. The Richland Beacon, whose short item was reprinted by other Louisiana papers, treated it as the latest in a run of such shootings and demanded arrests.

episodes.title: Lynchings of religious reformers in central Arkansas (1880)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynchings of religious reformers in central Arkansas were a series of killings in 1880 of men implicated in murders attributed to a religious reformation that had begun there that summer. They are known only from brief retrospective passages in April 1881 wire reports about Rev. Robert Matlock, one of the movement's leaders, which named none of the men lynched. The dispatches credited the lynchings with having ended the movement.

episodes.title: Lynching of the gambler Jim in a Colorado mining town
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of the gambler Jim was the hanging of a prisoner by a self-described "committee" in an unnamed Colorado mining town, some months before late November 1880. According to the only account, fifteen or twenty men took him from a guarded lockup while a coroner's jury sat over the police officer he was accused of shooting, and hanged him from a beam over a sidewalk. The story is known from a single recollection by a Pittsburgh oil inspector named Ramsey, which ran in several papers as a sketch of Western life.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Harry Hyath
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Harry Hyath took place in Des Moines, Iowa, on or before 1 September 1881, when a crowd at police headquarters decided to lynch Hyath, a boarder who had been arrested for allegedly attempting to outrage a seven-year-old girl. Police quickly placed him in jail, and he was discharged at his examination when the girl was too frightened to testify. The episode is known only from a short wire paragraph that two Minnesota weeklies printed in their crime columns, and it does not give Hyath's race.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Jack Byrd
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Jack Byrd was a failed effort to lynch a man accused of attempting to outrage a young lady in Rockingham County, Virginia, some time before February 1881. Byrd escaped, was convicted, and was received at the state penitentiary in Richmond on about February 24, 1881. The episode is known only from a single brief in the Richmond Daily Dispatch, which treated it as a passing detail in a report of his arrival at the prison.

episodes.title: Mob assault on Mr. Love, Somerset, Kentucky
episodes.lead: The mob assault on Mr. Love was an attack in or near Somerset, Kentucky, reported in January 1881, in which a mob led by Love's wife chased him and left him hanging head downward from a tree. Love survived after a preacher cut him down about two hours later, almost frozen. The episode is known only from a short, unsigned paragraph that white newspapers in at least ten states reprinted as a curiosity about how Somerset treated "faithless husbands."

episodes.title: Reported cow-carcass punishment in Morehouse Parish, Louisiana
episodes.lead: The reported cow-carcass punishment in Morehouse Parish, Louisiana, was an incident described in late summer 1881 in which unnamed men were said to have sewn a Black man accused of cow theft inside the carcass of a disemboweled cow. The story originated as a rumor in the Richland Beacon, and its location and truth were disputed by residents of the parish ward it named.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching in Chippewa County, Wisconsin
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching in Chippewa County, Wisconsin, was an attempt by a crowd in that county to lynch an unnamed young man, who escaped from them, at some time before April 1881. It is known only from a news brief on the Wisconsin House of Representatives' rejection of a bill to restore the death penalty, which named the attempt as the origin of that effort.

episodes.title: Shooting of Canless Blair
episodes.lead: The shooting of Canless Blair took place in or near Shelby, Cleveland County, North Carolina, in May 1882, when a sheriff's officer, B. F. Logan, wounded Blair, a Black man said to be an escaped convict, with rifle fire. A pistol shot that Blair was said to have fired at the officers struck George Wright, another Black man, in the leg. Blair survived and was jailed; the two papers that reported it told the officers' version.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of Ferguson at Charleston, Massachusetts
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of Ferguson at Charleston, Massachusetts, is known only from an editorial paragraph in the Benton Weekly Record of Benton, Montana, on June 29, 1882, which said that "Judge Lynch" had lately dealt with a man named Ferguson charged with outraging a widow and causing her death. The paragraph implied that Ferguson was killed but gave no date, description of the act, or race for anyone involved.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Geo. W. Randolph from Raleigh County, West Virginia
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Geo. W. Randolph was the beating and driving out of a Black schoolteacher by a mob in Raleigh County, West Virginia, reported in February 1882. According to Randolph's own statement, the mob beat him and ordered him to leave after a justice acquitted men he had had arrested, and he left to save his life. A Parkersburg paper headed its notice of the case "SHAMEFUL" while qualifying its comment on whether the statement was true.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Patrick Simpson
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Patrick Simpson was a pair of mob threats in 1881 against a man from Fulton, New York, who had been brought to Richmond, Kentucky, under arrest after he was mistaken for a fugitive murderer named Rogers. A mob tried to lynch him when he arrived, and after a court discharged him a crowd surrounded the court-house; he escaped on foot and reached home about the start of 1882. Papers told it as a story of mistaken identity and a narrow escape, and none of them gave Simpson's race.

episodes.title: Lynching of Peter Corbin
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Peter Corbin was the reported killing of a prisoner taken from the Gilmer county jail at Ellijay, Georgia, by a party of masked men in early 1882. Corbin, charged with an outrage on a lady, was reported found the next day in woods near the town with his head severed from his body. The only account is a short item from the Dalton Citizen, which passed the story on as something it had learned and hoped was untrue.

episodes.title: Logan saloon murder lynching
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
episodes.lead: The Logan saloon murder lynching was the killing by townsfolk of an unnamed man accused of murder in a drinking saloon at Logan, a Mormon settlement, at an unstated date before June 1882. It is known only from a single sentence in a June 1882 newspaper summary of a New York World correspondent's account of the town, which presented the lynching and the liquor ban that followed as part of the settlers' record of good order.
